---
title: "Classic Formations: I, Power I, Pro Set, Singleback, and Their Ancestors"
subtitle: "The quarterback under center and the backs behind him: eleven formations, what each one was built to do, why most of them faded, and why a few are coming back."
description: "How to recognize and name the classic under-center formations (the T, the pro set, the I-formation, offset I and Power I, singleback and ace, the wishbone, flexbone and Wing-T, and the goal-line formation), what problem each was invented to solve (a lead blocker, downhill angles, balance, misdirection), how they descend from one another, why two-back, under-center football declined in the NFL, where it survives in 2025, and which personnel grouping goes with which formation."
glossary:
  "T-formation": "A formation with the quarterback under center and three running backs side by side about four to five yards behind him, the ancestor of almost every modern under-center formation. Its modern form spread through football after 1940."
  "Full house backfield": "Any backfield with three running backs behind a quarterback who is under center (four players in the backfield in all), as in the T-formation, the wishbone and the Power I. Today it is mostly a goal-line and short-yardage look."
  "Pro set": {def: "A two-back formation with the quarterback under center and the halfback and fullback side by side behind him, usually with a tight end, a flanker and a split end (21 personnel). The standard NFL formation of the 1950s to the 1970s.", aliases: ["Split backs"]}
  "I-formation": "A two-back formation with the quarterback under center, the fullback directly behind him (about 4-5 yards deep) and the tailback directly behind the fullback (about 7 yards deep), so the three form an 'I'. Usually 21 personnel."
  "Offset I": {def: "An I-formation in which the fullback lines up a yard or two to one side, behind a guard or tackle, instead of directly behind the quarterback, to give him a better angle to where he will block. Offset toward the tight end it is often called a Strong I; offset away from him, a Weak I.", aliases: ["Strong I", "Weak I"]}
  "Power I": "An I-formation with a third back lined up beside the fullback, giving the offense two lead blockers in front of the tailback (usually 31 personnel). A short-yardage and goal-line formation."
  "Singleback": "Any formation with exactly one running back, lined up directly behind a quarterback who is under center, usually about seven yards deep. The second back of older formations becomes a tight end or a receiver."
  "Ace formation": "A singleback formation with two tight ends, one on each side of the line, and two wide receivers (12 personnel), balanced so the defense cannot tell which side is strong."
  "Wishbone": "A three-back option formation: the fullback close behind the quarterback and two halfbacks deeper and wider, one on each side, so the backfield looks like an upside-down Y. Built for the triple option; invented at Texas in 1968."
  "Flexbone": "An option formation that grew out of the wishbone: one fullback behind the quarterback, two slotbacks just off the line behind and outside the tackles, and two wide receivers on the line, usually with no tight end. Long the offense of Navy, Air Force and Army, and of Georgia Tech under Paul Johnson."
  "Wing-T": "A formation and system that mixes the T with the single wing: a fullback behind the quarterback, a halfback beside him, and a wingback just outside and behind the tight end. Built for misdirection, so that every play starts with the same backfield action."
  "Goal-line formation": "The offense's heaviest formation, used inside the 2- or 3-yard line and on short yardage: quarterback under center, two backs, three tight ends (or extra linemen) and no wide receivers, everyone aligned tight to the ball with narrow splits (23 personnel, or 14, or a jumbo grouping)."
---

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared helpers and the formation plates)"
#| output: false
import os

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, FancyBboxPatch, Rectangle, RegularPolygon

from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, defense, technique, style, show_animation
from gridiron.formations import LINE_D, OFF_BALL, TE_W, WING_W, OL_SPLIT

style.apply()

RB_RING = style.THIRD          # aqua ring: a running back of any kind (tailback, fullback, halfback, wingback)
TE_RING = style.LINE_TO_GAIN   # gold ring: a tight end
THREAT = "#0f7a55"             # darker aqua for "this back could go here" arrows (safe for text)
FAKE = style.MUTED             # gray for a back's fake in the Wing-T series panels
UC, FB_D, TB_D = -1.9, -4.5, -7.0   # quarterback under center, fullback and tailback depths (yards)
GL_SPLIT = 1.25                # goal-line splits: tighter than the normal OL_SPLIT (1.6)
DL_LABELS = {"SDE": "E", "WDE": "E", "SDT": "T", "WDT": "T"}


def line5(split=OL_SPLIT):
    """The five offensive linemen; only the center is lettered."""
    return [Player(k, k, "off", LINE_D, w, label=("C" if k == "C" else ""))
            for k, w in [("LT", -2 * split), ("LG", -split), ("C", 0.0), ("RG", split), ("RT", 2 * split)]]


def P(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    """An offensive skill player at (d, w): d = yards from the ball (negative = backfield),
    w = yards to the offense's right."""
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label or key)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def ring_by_body(p, skip=()):
    """Ring every back (aqua) and tight end (gold), as in the personnel chapter: count rings = personnel."""
    for k, pl in p.players.items():
        if k in skip or pl.side != "off":
            continue
        if pl.pos in ("RB", "FB"):
            p.highlight(k, color=RB_RING)
        elif pl.pos == "TE":
            p.highlight(k, color=TE_RING)
    return p


def hide_yard_numbers(ax):
    """Drop the faint painted field numbers (they sit where receivers stand in zoomed plates)."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() is not None and abs(t.get_alpha() - 0.55) < 1e-6:
            t.remove()


QB = P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q")
Y = P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W)

# The eleven classic formations, strength to the offense's right. Each is legal: seven men on the
# line (five linemen plus the two ends), only the ends of the line and the backs eligible.
# Letters: R = the running back (tailback), F = fullback, H = halfback (a third back), A/B = the
# flexbone's own back letters, W = the Wing-T wingback; Y and U = tight ends (in the goal-line set the
# third tight end, at the wing, is H, the H-back); X and Z = wide receivers; H in the singleback = slot.
# name: (typical personnel, one-line description, skill players)
FORMS = {
    "T-formation": ("32", "three backs side by side", [
        QB, P("LH", "RB", -4.6, -3.0, "H"), P("FB", "FB", -4.6, 0, "F"), P("RH", "RB", -4.6, 3.0, "H"),
        Y, P("U", "TE", LINE_D, -TE_W)]),
    "Pro set": ("21", "two backs side by side", [
        QB, P("HB", "RB", -5.0, -2.2, "H"), P("FB", "FB", -5.0, 2.2, "F"),
        Y, P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -14.0), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 13.0)]),
    "I-formation": ("21", "two backs stacked", [
        QB, P("FB", "FB", FB_D, 0, "F"), P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R"),
        Y, P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -14.0), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 13.0)]),
    "Offset I": ("21", "fullback cheated to one side", [
        QB, P("FB", "FB", FB_D, 1.6, "F"), P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R"),
        Y, P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -14.0), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 13.0)]),
    "Power I": ("31", "an I plus a halfback", [
        QB, P("FB", "FB", FB_D, 0, "F"), P("HB", "RB", FB_D, 2.1, "H"), P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R"),
        Y, P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -14.0)]),
    "Singleback": ("11", "one back, seven yards deep", [
        QB, P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R"), Y, P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -14.0),
        P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -8.5), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 13.0)]),
    "Ace": ("12", "one back, a tight end each side", [
        QB, P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R"), Y, P("U", "TE", LINE_D, -TE_W),
        P("X", "WR", OFF_BALL, -13.0), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 13.0)]),
    "Wishbone": ("31", "fullback close, halfbacks wide", [
        QB, P("FB", "FB", -3.9, 0, "F"), P("LH", "RB", -5.3, -3.1, "H"), P("RH", "RB", -5.3, 3.1, "H"),
        Y, P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -14.0)]),
    "Flexbone": ("30", "one back, two slotbacks", [
        QB, P("FB", "FB", -4.6, 0, "B"), P("LA", "RB", -1.6, -5.2, "A"), P("RA", "RB", -1.6, 5.2, "A"),
        P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -12.0, "X"), P("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 12.0, "Z")]),
    "Wing-T": ("31", "fullback, halfback, wingback", [
        QB, P("FB", "FB", FB_D, 0, "F"), P("HB", "RB", FB_D, -3.2, "H"), P("WB", "RB", OFF_BALL, WING_W + 1.2, "W"),
        Y, P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -12.0)]),
    "Goal line": ("23", "three tight ends, two backs", [
        QB, P("FB", "FB", FB_D, 0, "F"), P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R"),
        P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 3.9), P("U", "TE", LINE_D, -3.9), P("W", "TE", OFF_BALL, 5.2, "H")]),
}
SPLITS = {"Goal line": GL_SPLIT}


def players_of(name, mirror=False):
    pl = line5(SPLITS.get(name, OL_SPLIT)) + [q.moved() for q in FORMS[name][2]]
    return [q.mirrored() for q in pl] if mirror else pl


def check_legal(players):
    """Seven on the line, and every eligible receiver on the line is at an end of it."""
    off = [q for q in players if q.side == "off"]
    on = sorted([q for q in off if q.d > -1.0], key=lambda q: q.w)
    assert len(on) == 7, [q.key for q in on]
    for q in on[1:-1]:
        assert q.pos not in ("WR", "TE", "RB", "FB"), f"covered receiver {q.key}"


for _name in FORMS:
    check_legal(players_of(_name))


def plate(ax, name, lateral=(-16.5, 16.5), window=(-9.0, 2.8), mirror=False, sub=True, title=None):
    """One atlas plate: the formation alone, backs ringed aqua and tight ends gold."""
    code, desc, _ = FORMS[name]
    p = ring_by_body(Play(players_of(name, mirror), None, los=35, to_go=None))
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=lateral, window=window, title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    ax.text(0.0, 1.03, title or name, transform=ax.transAxes, ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=10,
            fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
    if sub:
        ax.text(1.0, 1.03, f"{code} personnel · {desc}", transform=ax.transAxes, ha="right",
                va="bottom", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK_2)
    return p, fld


def ring_legend(fig, y=0.0, ncol=3, extra=()):
    h = [Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", ms=9, markerfacecolor=style.OFFENSE, markeredgecolor=RB_RING,
                markeredgewidth=2.2, label="aqua ring: a running back"),
         Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", ms=9, markerfacecolor=style.OFFENSE, markeredgecolor=TE_RING,
                markeredgewidth=2.2, label="gold ring: a tight end"),
         Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", ms=9, markerfacecolor=style.OFFENSE, markeredgecolor="white",
                label="no ring: receiver, QB (Q), linemen")]
    h += list(extra)
    fig.legend(handles=h, loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, y), ncol=ncol, fontsize=7.3,
               frameon=False, handletextpad=0.3, columnspacing=1.1)


def plate_pair(a, b, mirror=(False, False), height=2.05):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, height))
    out = [plate(ax, n, mirror=m) for ax, n, m in zip(axes, (a, b), mirror)]
    fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.86, bottom=0.16, wspace=0.05)
    ring_legend(fig)
    return fig, out


def XY(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def label(fld, p, text, at, target=None, ha="center", fs=7.3, color=style.INK, va="center"):
    """A short boxed label at (d, w); with `target`, a thin leader line to that spot."""
    x, y = XY(fld, p, *at)
    box = dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.22", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.6)
    if target is None:
        fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fs, ha=ha, va=va, color=color, zorder=12, bbox=box)
    else:
        tx, ty = XY(fld, p, *target)
        fld.ax.annotate(text, xy=(tx, ty), xytext=(x, y), fontsize=fs, ha=ha, va=va, color=color,
                        zorder=12, bbox=box,
                        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.7, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=7))


def threat(fld, p, pts, color=THREAT, lw=1.7, text=None, text_at=None, fs=7.0, ls=(0, (3, 2))):
    """A dashed 'this back could go here' arrow through absolute (d, w) points."""
    xs, ys = XY(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    fld.ax.plot(xs[:-1], ys[:-1], color=color, lw=lw, ls=ls, zorder=6, solid_capstyle="round")
    fld.ax.plot(xs[-2:], ys[-2:], color=color, lw=lw, ls=ls, zorder=6)
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2] + 0.75 * (xs[-1] - xs[-2]), ys[-2] + 0.75 * (ys[-1] - ys[-2])),
                                     (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10, color=color,
                                     lw=lw, zorder=6))
    if text:
        x, y = XY(fld, p, *(text_at or pts[-1]))
        fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fs, color=color, fontweight="bold", ha="center", va="center",
                    zorder=9, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.92))


def base43(off, shell="two_high", fix=None):
    """A base 4-3 (four linemen, three linebackers, four defensive backs) aligned to `off`."""
    dfn = defense("4-3_over", shell, off)
    fix = fix or {}
    dfn = [q.moved(**fix[q.key]) if q.key in fix else q for q in dfn]
    return [q.moved(label=DL_LABELS.get(q.key, q.label)) for q in dfn]


# --- frame strips (PDF) and video (web), cropped to the box so the markers stay legible --------------
# gridiron's frame_strip fits all 22 players and has no rings; these panels zoom on the box, ring the
# backs the reader should follow, and put a one-line note under each frame.
MARK_R = 0.62


def pdf_build():
    return os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")


def tracking(play):
    df = play.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"].astype(str)
    return df


def panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings=()):
    """One moment of a simulated play: markers, trails of on-screen players, rings on chosen players."""
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[0], play.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window, numbers=False, hashes=False,
                lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=play.to_go)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    shown = cur[cur["x"].between(play.los + window[0] + 0.8, play.los + window[1] - 0.8)
                & cur["y"].between(ylo + 0.8, yhi - 0.8)]
    ids = set(shown["_id"])
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(ids) & (df["side"] != "ball")]
    for (_, side), g in trails.groupby(["_id", "side"]):
        xs, ys = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.4, zorder=3)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for _, r in shown.iterrows():
        x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(r["x"], r["y"]))
        if r["side"] == "ball":     # the ball, drawn small and just ahead of whoever holds it
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x + 0.75, y + 0.55), 0.6, 0.36, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=11))
            continue
        lab = str(r.get("label", "") or "")
        if r["side"] == "off":
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), MARK_R, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=8))
            tc = "white"
        else:
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=MARK_R * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                        fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=8))
            tc = style.INK
        fs = max(4.0, min(8.0, ppy * (0.85 if len(lab) <= 1 else 0.62)))
        ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
    for key, col in rings:
        r = cur[cur["displayName"] == key].iloc[0]
        x, y = fld.xy(r["x"], r["y"])
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 1.05, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.7, zorder=7))
    return fld


def strip(play, times, lateral, window, notes=None, rings=(), ncols=2, width_in=6.5):
    """Numbered frame strip with a fixed, box-sized window and a note under each frame."""
    df = tracking(play)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(times) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False,
                             figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + (0.6 if notes else 0.25))))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(times):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times)):
        panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings)
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  " + ("snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s"),
                     fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK_2, loc="left")
        if notes:
            ax.text(0.5, -0.03, notes[i], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top",
                    fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.4 if notes else 0.6, w_pad=0.6)
    return fig


def video(play, times, lateral, window, notes=None, rings=(), width_in=5.2):
    """Web version of the strip: the same panel at every frame, with the strip's notes as captions."""
    import shutil
    from matplotlib import animation
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    df = tracking(play)
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * span_d / span_w + 0.4))
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()

    def update(fid):
        ax.clear()
        t = float(tmap[fid])
        panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings)
        txt = ("snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s")
        if notes:
            cur = [n for tt, n in zip(times, notes) if tt <= t + 1e-6]
            txt += ("   " + cur[-1].replace("\n", " ")) if cur else ""
        ax.set_title(txt, fontsize=9, color=style.INK, loc="left")
        return []

    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=sorted(df["frameId"].unique()), interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def animation_or_strip(play, times, **kw):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF."""
    if pdf_build():
        strip(play, times, **kw)
        plt.show()
    else:
        kw.pop("ncols", None)
        video(play, times, **kw)
```

Picture a third-and-1 for the 2024 Baltimore Ravens, late in a close game. The Ravens break the
huddle and something about the picture looks old. The quarterback walks right up behind
the center and puts his hands under him. Behind him, in a straight line, stand a 300-pound
fullback and, seven yards deep, a 247-pound running back, hands on knees. One tight end, two
receivers. The analyst says "they're in the I," and the defense, which has spent most of the
afternoon with five defensive backs on the field, is already shouting and pointing and walking a
safety down toward the line. This is a formation your grandfather would recognize. So why is one of
the best offenses in football still using it, and why does the defense react as if it already knows
what's coming? This chapter is about those old shapes: what each was built to do, how they grew out
of one another, why most of them faded from the NFL, and why the ones that survived are making a
comeback.

**You'll be able to…**

- Name the classic formations on sight: the I-formation, offset I, Power I, pro set (split backs),
  singleback, ace, T-formation, wishbone, flexbone, Wing-T and the goal-line formation.
- Say what each formation was invented to do (give the runner a lead blocker, let him run
  downhill, stay balanced, or fool the defense with misdirection) and what it gives up.
- Match each formation to the personnel grouping that usually comes with it.
- Explain why two-back, under-center football declined in the NFL, and point to the three places it
  survives in 2025: 21 personnel, short yardage and play-action.
- Use the backfield as a pre-snap clue: under center or shotgun, one back or two, stacked, split or
  offset, and count blockers against the defenders near the ball.

## Reading a formation from the back to the front

The [personnel](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd) told you *who* is on the field. The
*formation* tells you *where they stand*. [Formation Rules and the Language of
Alignment](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) gave you the grammar: seven players on the
line of scrimmage, the ends of the line eligible to catch passes, the receiver letters (X, Y, Z,
H, F), and the quarterback's three depths, [under center](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd)
(taking the snap directly from the center's hands), the
[pistol](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) (about three to four yards back) and the
[shotgun](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) (about five yards back). This chapter and
[the next](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd) are the vocabulary: the named formations
you'll actually hear on a broadcast.

The classic formations share one thing: **the quarterback is under center.** For most of football
history that was simply how the game was played, and the formations differ mainly in what stands
*behind* the quarterback. So read them from the back to the front:

1. **Is the quarterback under center?** If he is, you're in this chapter's world.
2. **How many backs, and how are they arranged?** One or two or three; stacked one behind another,
   side by side, or one shifted to the side.
3. **Where are the tight ends and receivers?** A tight end on one side or both, a wing, receivers
   wide.

One rule settles most arguments about step 2. **Name the formation by where players stand; count the
personnel by who they are.** Anyone a yard or more behind the line and inside the width of the tight
ends is in the backfield, so a tight end standing directly behind the quarterback makes the formation
an I, whoever he is. The personnel comes from the substitution, as in
[Personnel](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd): from the couch you can't tell a tight end from a fullback
by where he stands, and often not by his build. When the two disagree, say both: a tight end at
fullback is "an I with 12 personnel." The same rule explains the exceptions you'll meet below. The
Wing-T's wingback and the flexbone's slotbacks stand near the line but are running backs, so they
count as backs; an H-back is a tight end wherever he stands.

Here is the most famous answer to those three questions, labeled part by part.

```{python}
#| label: fig-anatomy
#| fig-cap: "Anatomy of a classic formation: the I-formation (21 personnel). The quarterback (Q) is under center; the fullback (F) stands about 4–5 yards deep, directly behind him; the tailback (R, the running back) about 7 yards deep, directly behind the fullback. Seven men are on the line: the split end (X), the five linemen (only the center, C, is lettered) and the tight end (Y). The flanker (Z) stands a yard off the line, so Y, not Z, is the right end of the line and is eligible. Aqua rings mark backs, the gold ring the tight end."
p = ring_by_body(Play(players_of("I-formation"), None, los=35, to_go=None))
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-18.5, 18.5), window=(-10.5, 6.5), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(fld.ax)
label(fld, p, "split end (X):\non the line", (3.6, -13.0), target=(LINE_D, -14.0))
label(fld, p, "seven on the line:\nX, five linemen, Y", (3.6, -2.0))
label(fld, p, "tight end (Y)", (3.6, 6.2), target=(LINE_D, TE_W))
label(fld, p, "flanker (Z): a yard\noff the line", (3.6, 14.0), target=(OFF_BALL, 13.0))
label(fld, p, "quarterback (Q) under center:\nhands under the center", (-3.4, -7.6), target=(UC, 0.0))
label(fld, p, "fullback (F): 4–5 yards deep,\nthe lead blocker", (-4.9, 10.2), target=(FB_D, 0.0))
label(fld, p, "tailback (R): about 7 yards deep,\nsees the blocks, runs downhill", (-7.6, 10.2),
      target=(TB_D, 0.0))
plt.show()
```

Every formation in this chapter can be described in those same terms, and the names often tell you
the shape. The *I* is a letter. The *T* is a letter (the quarterback and three backs form the
crossbar and stem). The *wishbone* looks like one. The *pro set* was what the pros used. The
naming isn't standardized, and every team has its own playbook words, but the broadcast names are
stable enough to learn once.

**The letters in this chapter's diagrams.** Playbook letters get reused, so here is the key, and it
never changes inside a figure. On offense (circles): **Q** quarterback, **C** center, **R** the running
back (the tailback), **F** fullback, **H** a halfback (a third back in the old formations), **X** and
**Z** wide receivers, **Y** and **U** tight ends. Two letters do double duty, as they do in real
playbooks: in the one-back pictures **H** is the "move" player from [Formation
Rules](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd), a slot receiver or an H-back, and the option and
Wing-T formations bring their own back letters (A, B, W), named where they appear. The ring settles
it: **aqua is a running back, gold is a tight end, no ring is a receiver**. On defense (squares): **E**
end, **T** tackle, **N** nose tackle, **S**, **M** and **W** the Sam, Mike and Will linebackers, **C**
cornerback, **FS** and **SS** the safeties.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In *Madden* you pick a formation from a menu ("I-Form Pro," "Singleback Ace," "Strong Close") and
then pick a play from the list that belongs to that formation, as if each formation owned its own
plays. Real offenses work the other way around. A team has a few dozen run and pass plays and
**runs most of them from many formations**, because a play the defense can predict from the
formation is a play the defense can stop. The formation is the first word of the play call ("I
Right 26 Power," as [What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd)
spelled out), not the play. The menu names themselves are borrowed from real playbooks.
:::

## The ancestor: the T-formation

Almost every formation in this chapter descends from one shape. In the [**T-formation**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-t-formation)
the quarterback stands under center and three backs line up side by side about four or five
yards behind him: a fullback in the middle and a halfback on each side. Seen from the press box,
the quarterback and the line of backs make a T.

```{python}
#| label: fig-t-formation
#| fig-cap: "The T-formation (in modern terms, 32 personnel: three backs, two tight ends). Three backs stand side by side about 4½ yards deep, a halfback (H) on each side of the fullback (F), with the quarterback (Q) under center between them and the line. Four players in the backfield behind an under-center quarterback is a full house. Both ends (Y and U) are tight, as in the 1940s; there is no wide receiver at all."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.0))
p, fld = plate(ax, "T-formation", lateral=(-13.5, 13.5), window=(-9.6, 3.2))
label(fld, p, "full house: three backs plus\nan under-center quarterback", (-7.4, 7.6), target=(-4.6, 3.0))
label(fld, p, "a back in the middle\nand one on each side", (-7.6, -6.6), target=(-4.6, 0.0))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.9, bottom=0.03)
plt.show()
```

The backs' names are older than the T itself, which is why they're confusing: the
[fullback](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd) is the bigger, blocking-first back, and the
[halfbacks](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd) are the runners. Any backfield with three
backs behind an under-center quarterback, four players in all, is called a [**full house
backfield**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-full-house-backfield). The T is the original full house;
you'll meet two more in this chapter (the Power I and the wishbone), and you'll still see one on the
goal line most Sundays.

### Why it exists: speed to the line

The T's predecessor was the [single wing](../11-history/11-01-single-wing-to-scoring-drought.qmd),
the dominant formation of the 1910s to the 1930s, in which the center snapped the ball several yards
back, through the air, to a tailback who ran, passed or handed off. The single wing is a power
formation, but it's slow: a direct snap takes time, the runner starts from a standstill several
yards deep, and the defense can see who has the ball.

The T fixed all three problems with one change, **putting the quarterback's hands under the
center.** A hand-to-hand snap is instant and almost never fumbled. The quarterback can turn and hand
the ball to a back who is already running, so the ball carrier hits the line of scrimmage at full
speed one or two seconds after the snap. And because the quarterback can fake a handoff to one back
and give to another with his back to the defense, nobody across the line knows for sure who has the
ball. With three backs, all a few strides from the line and facing forward, the T threatens the
middle and both flanks on every snap, and the defense has to respect all of them.

The modern T arrived with a bang. Coaches had used a tight T for decades, but in 1940 Clark
Shaughnessy's version of it, with wider splits, quicker hitting plays and a back sent in motion
before the snap, went undefeated at Stanford, and George Halas's Chicago Bears, who had been
developing the same ideas with Shaughnessy's help, used it to beat Washington **73–0** in the NFL
Championship Game on December 8, 1940.[^tform] Within a decade almost every team in the NFL had
switched; the Pittsburgh Steelers, the last NFL holdout, used the single wing for the
last time in 1952 and switched to the T in 1953.[^steelers] [The Single Wing to the Scoring
Drought](../11-history/11-01-single-wing-to-scoring-drought.qmd) tells that history in full; what
matters here is that the T is the trunk of the tree.

What did the T give up? **Width.** With both ends tight and three backs packed behind the
quarterback, it had no receivers outside the formation, so the defense could pack its own players
near the ball too. Most of what happened next is the story of coaches taking the T and pulling one
of its players out wide.

## The family tree

The diagram below is the map for the rest of the chapter. Each branch is an answer to the question
"what should we do with the T's three backs?" Some coaches stacked them, some split them, some
spread them out, some kept all three and taught the quarterback to read the defense instead of
blocking it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-family-tree
#| fig-cap: "The family tree of the classic formations (dates are when each became prominent, not the first time anyone drew it; several are disputed, see the text). Each icon shows the line (gray), the player who takes the snap (dark blue), the backs (aqua) and any tight end or end close to the line (gold). In the single wing the dark-blue dot is the blocking back: the snap went past him, through the air, to the tailback. In the split-T the line itself is spread. Blue boxes are formations you can still see in today's NFL; gray boxes mostly live on in college, high school, the service academies or the history books (the full-house T survives only as an occasional goal-line look). The shotgun has two parents: the one-back passing sets, and the single wing's direct snap (dashed)."
from matplotlib.patches import Circle as _C

def glyph(ax, cx, cy, players, s=0.092):
    """A tiny backfield icon: line, quarterback, backs, close tight ends (receivers wider than 8 yd dropped)."""
    for q in players:
        if abs(q.w) > 8.0:
            continue
        x, y = cx + q.w * s, cy + q.d * s
        if q.pos in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
            fc, ec = style.BASELINE, style.BASELINE
        elif q.pos == "QB":
            fc, ec = style.OFFENSE_DARK, style.OFFENSE_DARK
        elif q.pos in ("RB", "FB"):
            fc, ec = style.THIRD, style.THIRD
        elif q.pos == "TE":
            fc, ec = style.LINE_TO_GAIN, style.LINE_TO_GAIN
        else:
            fc, ec = style.OFFENSE, style.OFFENSE
        ax.add_patch(_C((x, y), 0.62 * s, fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=0.5, zorder=5))

SINGLE_WING = [Player(k, k, "off", LINE_D, w) for k, w in
               [("LT", -1.6), ("LG", 0.0), ("C", 1.6), ("RG", 3.2), ("RT", 4.8)]] + [
    P("SE", "TE", LINE_D, -3.2), P("TE2", "TE", LINE_D, 6.4),                # seven on the line, unbalanced
    P("BB", "QB", -1.2, 2.6, "B"), P("TB", "RB", -5.0, 0.6), P("FB", "FB", -4.3, 2.6),
    P("WB", "RB", -1.2, 8.0)]   # direct snap to the tailback; the blocking back (dark blue) is not a passer
SHOTGUN = line5() + [P("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", -5.0, -2.1, "R"), Y]
SPLIT_T = line5(2.3) + [P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("LH", "RB", -4.6, -3.0, "H"), P("FB", "FB", -4.6, 0, "F"),
                        P("RH", "RB", -4.6, 3.0, "H"), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 6.9), P("U", "TE", LINE_D, -6.9)]
# the split-T's "split" is the line: splits of roughly a yard or more between linemen

NODES = {  # key: (title, years, x, y, players, still in the NFL?)
    "sw":   ("Single wing", "1900s–1930s", 1.3, 8.35, SINGLE_WING, False),
    "t":    ("T-formation", "modern T, 1940", 5.0, 8.35, players_of("T-formation"), False),
    "splt": ("Split-T", "1941, wide line splits", 3.75, 5.95, SPLIT_T, False),
    "wingt": ("Wing-T", "1950", 1.3, 5.95, players_of("Wing-T"), False),
    "pro":  ("Pro set", "1950s", 6.25, 5.95, players_of("Pro set"), True),
    "i":    ("I-formation", "1950s–60s", 8.7, 5.95, players_of("I-formation"), True),
    "bone": ("Wishbone", "1968, after the veer", 3.75, 3.55, players_of("Wishbone"), False),
    "one":  ("Singleback / ace", "1980s", 6.25, 3.55, players_of("Ace"), True),
    "powi": ("Offset I, Power I", "1960s–70s", 8.7, 3.55, players_of("Power I"), True),
    "flex": ("Flexbone", "1980s", 3.75, 1.15, players_of("Flexbone"), False),
    "gun":  ("Shotgun and spread", "the next chapter", 6.25, 1.15, SHOTGUN, True),
}
EDGES = [("sw", "t"), ("sw", "wingt"), ("t", "splt"), ("t", "wingt"), ("t", "pro"), ("t", "i"),
         ("splt", "bone"), ("bone", "flex"), ("pro", "one"), ("i", "powi"), ("one", "gun")]
BW, BH = 2.2, 1.75

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 6.9))
ax.set_xlim(0, 10)
ax.set_ylim(-0.55, 9.4)
ax.axis("off")
for a, b in EDGES:
    (_, _, xa, ya, _, _), (_, _, xb, yb, _, _) = NODES[a], NODES[b]
    if abs(ya - yb) < 0.01:   # same row: side to side
        start, end = (xa + BW / 2 * np.sign(xb - xa), ya), (xb - BW / 2 * np.sign(xb - xa), yb)
    else:
        start, end = (xa, ya - BH / 2), (xb, yb + BH / 2)
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(start, end, arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10, color=style.MUTED, lw=1.1,
                                 connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.0", zorder=1, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=2))
for key, (title, years, x, y, pl, nfl_now) in NODES.items():
    ec = style.OFFENSE if nfl_now else style.MUTED
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x - BW / 2, y - BH / 2), BW, BH, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=0.12",
                                fc=style.SURFACE, ec=ec, lw=1.6 if nfl_now else 1.0, zorder=2))
    glyph(ax, x, y + 0.62, pl)
    ax.text(x, y - 0.32, title, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.2, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK,
            zorder=6)
    ax.text(x, y - 0.66, years, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, zorder=6)
ax.text(1.3, 3.55, "its series lives on in\njet sweeps and\nmisdirection (Part 3)", ha="center", va="center",
        fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, style="italic")
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((1.3, 5.95 - BH / 2), (1.3, 4.15), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10,
                             color=style.MUTED, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (3, 2))))
ax.text(8.7, 1.15, "where two-back\nfootball survives:\n21 personnel, short\nyardage, play-action",
        ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, style="italic")
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((8.7, 3.55 - BH / 2), (8.7, 1.85), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10,
                             color=style.MUTED, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (3, 2))))
# the shotgun's second parent: the single wing's direct snap (Red Hickey's 49ers, 1960)
ax.plot([1.3 - BW / 2, 0.12, 0.12, 6.25, 6.25], [8.35, 8.35, -0.2, -0.2, 1.15 - BH / 2 - 0.12],
        color=style.MUTED, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((6.25, 0.0), (6.25, 1.15 - BH / 2), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10,
                             color=style.MUTED, lw=1.1, zorder=1))
ax.text(3.2, -0.2, "the direct snap returns: the shotgun, 1960", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7,
        color=style.INK_2, style="italic", bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
h = [Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.6, label="still seen in the NFL"),
     Line2D([], [], color=style.MUTED, lw=1.0, label="mostly college, high school or history")]
ax.legend(handles=h, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.62, 1.035), ncol=2, fontsize=7.5, frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

You don't need to memorize the dates. The useful thing is the logic of the branches, because each
one is a different answer to the same trade: **every player you keep in the backfield is a blocker
or a runner you gain, and a receiver you lose.**

Two names on the tree never get a section of their own, because here they matter only as links. The
*split-T* was Don Faurot's 1941 Missouri version of the T. Its "split" was the *line*: wide gaps
between the linemen that stretched the defensive front, while the quarterback rode down the line and
either kept the ball or pitched it to a trailing halfback, depending on what one unblocked defender
did. It may have been football's first option offense.[^splitt] The *veer* was Bill Yeoman's
triple-option attack at Houston from the mid-1960s, one of the offenses Emory Bellard was trying to
improve when he drew up the wishbone.[^veer] [Option Football](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd)
has both.

## The pro set: one back goes wide

The first big branch came from the passing game. In 1949 Shaughnessy, by then coaching the Los
Angeles Rams, took one of his T-formation halfbacks, Elroy "Crazylegs" Hirsch, and lined him up
wide as a receiver: a [flanker](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd).[^hirsch] (Others had split a back wide before, so
Hirsch's claim to be the *first* flanker is disputed, but he became the model for the position.) Two backs
stayed behind the quarterback, side by side.
Add a tight end on one side and a receiver split wide on the other, and you have the formation that
ran the NFL for the next quarter century.

The [**pro set**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pro-set), also called [**split
backs**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-split-backs), puts the quarterback under center and the
halfback and fullback side by side behind him, usually about five yards deep and roughly behind the
guards or tackles. Up front there's a tight end on one side, the [flanker
(Z)](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) a yard off the line on the tight end's side, and the
[split end (X)](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) on the line on the other side. That's 21
personnel: two backs, one tight end, two receivers.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pro-set
#| fig-cap: "The pro set (split backs, 21 personnel). Left: the plate. The halfback (H) and fullback (F) stand side by side about five yards deep; the tight end (Y) and flanker (Z) are on the right, the split end (X) on the left. Right: what the backfield threatens. Each back is close to a hole on his own side and can hit it quickly (the short dashed arrows), or release into the flat, the short area toward the sideline within a few yards of the line (shaded; it runs on to the sideline beyond this picture). The defense can't tell the play's direction from the backs' alignment, and both edges of the pass protection have a back beside them to pick up a blitzer."
PRO_WIN = (-10.4, 6.0)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 2.75))
p, fld = plate(axes[0], "Pro set", window=PRO_WIN)
p2, fld2 = plate(axes[1], "Pro set", sub=False, title="What it threatens", window=PRO_WIN)
for sgn in (-1, 1):
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = XY(fld2, p2, -0.5, sgn * 9.0), XY(fld2, p2, 4.5, sgn * 16.5)
    fld2.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(x0, x1), min(y0, y1)), abs(x1 - x0), abs(y1 - y0), fc=THREAT, alpha=0.10,
                                ec="none", zorder=1))
    threat(fld2, p2, [(-5.0, sgn * 2.2), (-2.6, sgn * 2.5), (1.4, sgn * 2.5)])
    threat(fld2, p2, [(-5.0, sgn * 2.2), (-4.0, sgn * 5.4), (-0.6, sgn * 8.6), (2.0, sgn * 10.4)])
    label(fld2, p2, "the flat", (3.6, sgn * 13.6), color=THREAT, fs=7.0)
label(fld2, p2, "a back each side:\nrun, block or catch", (-8.6, 0.0), color=THREAT)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.88, bottom=0.13, wspace=0.05)
ring_legend(fig)
plt.show()
```

### Why it exists: balance

The pro set's virtue is *balance*. With a back on each side of the quarterback, the offense can
run either way with a lead blocker, throw to either back in the flat, or keep both in to block a
blitz on either side. The defense gets almost no clue from the backfield, because the backfield
looks the same whichever way the play goes. Meanwhile the flanker and split end give the passing
game two real receivers outside, which the T never had. That combination, a credible run game both
ways plus two wide receivers and a tight end, made the pro set the standard NFL formation from the
late 1950s into the 1980s. Bill Walsh's early San Francisco offenses, the original [West Coast
offense](../04-the-passing-game/04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd), was built on split backs and threw many of its short passes to backs releasing from them.[^walsh]

What does it give up? **The deep tailback.** Split backs can hit a hole fast: each is only about five
yards deep and close to the line, and split-back dives and traps are among the quickest runs in
football. What they lose is the luxury of a back seven yards deep, directly behind the quarterback,
who has time to watch the blocks form and can cut to either side. And there's no lead blocker lined
up in front of the runner: if the play wants one, he has to come from the other side and cross the
ball carrier's path, which costs a beat and has to be timed so the two don't collide. For power
running straight at the defense, the next branch was better.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Green Bay Packers, 1959–1967"}
Vince Lombardi's Packers won five NFL championships in seven seasons (1961, 1962, 1965, 1966 and
1967, the last two followed by wins in the first two Super Bowls), and they did it mostly from the
pro set.[^lombardi] Fullback Jim Taylor and halfback Paul Hornung lined up side by side behind Bart
Starr, and the signature play was the *power sweep*: both guards (Jerry Kramer and Fuzzy Thurston)
pulled toward the sideline, the fullback blocked the defensive end, and the halfback took the
handoff wide behind a wall of blockers. Lombardi's name for the formation was "Red": split backs, set
wide apart. The runner didn't aim for a fixed hole; he followed his blockers and "ran to daylight,"
the title of Lombardi's 1963 book.

**What to notice:** the split backs are what made the sweep hard to diagnose. The same backfield ran
the sweep, the fullback's runs inside and the plays that punished defenses for chasing the sweep, and
the defense couldn't tell which from the backfield. (The sweep itself is drawn block by block in [Gap
and Power Runs](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd).)
:::

## The I-formation: stacking the backs

If you want the ball carrier running straight at the defense, put him directly behind the
quarterback, and put the blocker in front of him. That is the
[**I-formation**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-i-formation): quarterback under center, the
fullback directly behind him about four to five yards deep, and the tailback directly behind the
fullback about seven yards deep. Three players in a straight line make the I. With one tight end and
two receivers it's 21 personnel, and "I-formation" and "21 personnel" were close to synonyms for a
generation.

The I is usually credited to Tom Nugent at the Virginia Military Institute in 1950 (stacked
backfields appear in older playbooks too, so "invented" is disputed). It became famous at USC in the
1960s under John McKay, who got it from his assistant Don Coryell; McKay's I-formation tailbacks (Mike
Garrett, then O.J. Simpson) won Heisman Trophies and gave USC the nickname "Tailback U."[^ihist] By the
1970s and '80s it was everywhere, college and pro.

The deep tailback is the whole point. Seven yards is a long way back, and it buys three things.

**A running start.** The tailback takes the handoff already moving at speed, straight toward the
line: running [downhill](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd), as Formation Rules put it. A
runner who meets a linebacker at full speed going forward wins more collisions than one who meets him
moving sideways.

**Time to see.** From seven yards the tailback can watch the blocks form in front of him before he
commits. If the hole he was promised closes, he can see the one that opened instead. Because he's
centered, that includes the other side of the formation: he can press the play side and then
[cut back](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd) against the grain (turn back across the
formation into a lane the over-running defense left), which is why zone-running teams kept the I.

**A lead blocker.** The fullback is between the tailback and the line, so on a run he goes first,
into the hole, and blocks the first defender who fills it, usually a linebacker. That's a [lead
block](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd), and the simplest I-formation run of all,
the [iso](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd) (short for "isolation"), is built on it.
The diagram below draws it against a [base 4-3](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) defense: four
defensive linemen, three linebackers and four defensive backs, the defense's traditional starting
lineup.

Count before you look at the arrows, because this is the arithmetic of every running play. The
offense's possible **blockers** are everyone except the quarterback and the ball carrier: here the
five linemen, the tight end and the fullback, **seven**. The defenders who matter are the ones close
enough to the ball to tackle the runner in the first second, the ones in what [A First Look at
Defense](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) calls the *box* (roughly, from just outside one tight
end to just outside the other, and back about five to seven yards). The two cornerbacks are out
covering the wide receivers and the two safeties are 10 or more yards deep, so they don't count yet.
That leaves the four linemen and three linebackers: **seven**. Seven blockers for seven defenders
means every defender near the ball can be blocked, and the runner meets nobody unblocked until the
safeties arrive. Coaches call that a hat on a hat. When the defense has one more player in the box
than the offense has blockers, one defender is free, and the runner has to beat him. Keep that count
in mind; the rest of the chapter keeps using it.

In the iso, four linemen and the tight end block the man in front of them, the left guard climbs to the
Mike linebacker, and the fullback leads through the gap between the left guard and left tackle onto
the Will, "isolating" him, one on one. The tailback reads that block and runs off it. The iso and its
relatives are taught properly in [Gap and Power Runs](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd);
here it's the cleanest picture of why the I exists.

```{python}
#| label: fig-iso
#| fig-cap: "Why the I exists: the iso (isolation) run against a base 4-3. Seven blockers (five linemen, the tight end Y and the fullback F) for seven defenders in the box (four linemen and three linebackers): a hat on a hat. Four linemen and Y block the man in front of them; the left guard climbs to the Mike (M); the fullback (aqua ring) leads through the gap between the left guard and left tackle and blocks the Will (W, orange ring). That gap is the spot to attack: in this front no defensive lineman stands in it, only the Will. The tailback (R) takes the handoff about four yards deep, already moving forward, aims just inside the fullback and reads his block. The cornerbacks (C) and safeties (FS, SS) are too far away to count in the first second."
def iso_play(moving=False):
    """moving=True adds the blocked defenders' movement (the end driven out, the 1-technique driven
    off the ball) for the frame strip; the static diagram leaves them standing."""
    off = players_of("I-formation")
    dfn = base43(off, fix={"MIKE": dict(w=0.4), "SAM": dict(d=4.0, w=6.4), "WILL": dict(w=-3.0)})
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
    p.path("WILL", [(1.6, -2.9)], absolute=True, delay=0.35)          # the Will fills the hole
    p.path("MIKE", [(3.4, 0.6)], absolute=True, delay=0.35)           # the Mike steps up inside it
    if moving:
        p.path("WDE", [(1.6, -5.6)], absolute=True, delay=0.3, speed=1.5)  # the end, driven out by the tackle
        p.path("WDT", [(1.4, 0.5)], absolute=True, delay=0.3, speed=1.5)   # the 1-technique, driven by the center
    p.block("LT", target="WDE")
    p.block("C", target="WDT")
    p.block("RG", target="SDT")
    p.block("RT", target="SDE")
    p.block("Y", target="SAM")
    p.block("LG", target="MIKE", speed=3.4, delay=0.15)              # the left guard climbs to the Mike
    p.block("FB", pts=[(1.9, -1.9), (5.1, -2.85)], speed=6.0)         # the fullback leads to the Will
    p.path("QB", [(-3.0, 0.2)], absolute=True)                        # reverse out to hand off
    p.run("RB", [(-3.6, -1.0), (-0.5, -1.5), (2.5, -1.5), (9.0, -1.6)], absolute=True, delay=0.2)
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.75)
    p.highlight("FB", "RB", color=RB_RING)
    p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
    return p

iso = iso_play()
fld = iso.draw(lateral=(-17.5, 17.5), window=(-9.0, 15.0), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(fld.ax)
label(fld, iso, "fullback leads,\nblocks the Will", (5.2, -8.6), target=(0.6, -2.85))
label(fld, iso, "tailback follows,\nreads the block", (-5.8, -7.4), target=(-3.6, -1.0))
label(fld, iso, "7 blockers vs\n7 in the box", (-5.0, 8.5))
plt.show()
```

Watch the same play in motion. Notice how far the tailback has to travel before he gets the ball,
and how that distance is what lets him arrive at the line of scrimmage at full speed, a split second
after the fullback.

```{python}
#| label: fig-iso-strip
#| fig-cap: "The iso in motion (simulated, BDB-format tracking), zoomed on the box; the fullback (F) and tailback (R) are ringed in aqua, the ball is the small brown oval. 1: at the snap the fullback is already the closest back to the line. 2: he arrives at the line as the tailback takes the handoff about four yards deep. 3: the fullback has met the Will (W) in the hole and the left guard is on the Mike (M); the tailback, now at full speed, is right behind them. 4: the tailback is through the hole and past the linebackers, with only the safeties left. The faint trails show where everyone has been."
animation_or_strip(iso_play(moving=True), [0.0, 0.85, 1.35, 2.2], lateral=(-11.0, 11.0), window=(-8.5, 9.5),
                   rings=(("FB", RB_RING), ("RB", RB_RING)),
                   notes=["snap: F is closest to the line", "F arrives at the line; R gets the ball",
                          "F meets the Will; LG is on the Mike", "R is through, past the linebackers"])
```

### What the I gives up

Every strength of the I has a price.

- **It's slow to the edge.** A tailback seven yards deep has a long way to go to get around the end.
  Outside runs from the I take time, and a fast defense can beat them to the sideline.
- **The backs are slow to get into routes.** The fullback is in the middle of the formation and the
  tailback is deep; neither can get into a pass route quickly. On a straight dropback the I has
  really only three quick receivers (the two wideouts and the tight end), and the defense knows it.
  The exception proves the rule: on play-action, the fullback who "should" be blocking becomes a
  fourth receiver precisely because nobody is watching him.
- **It's obvious.** Two backs stacked behind an under-center quarterback says "run" loudly. In
  neutral situations (first and second down, game still close) from 2022 to 2025, NFL offenses lined
  up under center with two backs threw on only about 27% of plays, roughly three runs in four.
  With one back under center they threw about 38% of the time; from the shotgun with one back or
  none, about 71%.[^neutral] That's the price, and also, as you'll see, the opportunity.

### Offset I: cheating the fullback

A fullback directly behind the quarterback has to choose a side after the snap, and the defense
can't tell which side. That's good for disguise but bad for geometry: if the play goes wide, he has
to run sideways before he can block anyone. The [**offset I**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-offset-i)
moves the fullback a yard or two to one side, behind a guard or tackle, so he starts closer to where
he's needed.

```{python}
#| label: fig-i-family
#| fig-cap: "Two variations on the I. Left: the offset I, here offset to the strong (tight end) side, with the fullback (F) behind the right guard instead of directly behind the quarterback (a 'Strong I'). Right: the Power I, which adds a third back, a halfback (H), beside the fullback, so the tailback (R) has two lead blockers in front of him. Both are under center; the Power I gives up a receiver to do it (31 personnel)."
fig, out = plate_pair("Offset I", "Power I")
plt.show()
```

Coaches say the fullback is offset **strong** (toward the tight end) or **weak** (away from it).
Offset strong, he's in position to lead on runs to the tight end side, where the offense has an
extra blocker. Offset weak, he's in position to lead on runs away from the tight end, or to block a
blitzing linebacker coming from the weak side on a pass. The cost is a clue. A fullback offset to one
side tilts the offense toward that side, and defensive coaches study which way each opponent offsets
on which plays. Smart offenses run plays both ways from both offsets so the tilt means nothing.

Playbooks and broadcasts have their own words for these. An I offset strong is often a [**Strong
I**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-strong-i) and offset weak a [**Weak
I**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-weak-i) (*Madden* uses both). And a classic formation's full name is usually the
backfield plus the receivers: "I Pro" is the I with the tight end on one side and a receiver on each
side, as drawn here; "I Twins" puts both wide receivers on the side away from the tight end; "I
Slot" puts the flanker in the slot. When an analyst says "I-formation twins," he has told you the
backfield and then the receivers, back to front, exactly the order this chapter reads them. The
receiver sets get their own chapter: [Spread Formations](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd).

### Power I: two lead blockers

The [**Power I**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-power-i) adds a third back beside the
fullback, so the tailback has two blockers leading him: usually 31 personnel (three backs, one tight
end, one receiver), another full house. It's a short-yardage and goal-line formation, built for the
moment when the offense needs one yard and the defense knows it.

Do the count. The Power I has eight blockers (five linemen, the tight end and two lead backs), one
more than a base 4-3 has in the box. So the defense answers the way defenses always answer an extra
blocker: it brings a safety down, and it's eight against eight again. The extra back's job is to make
sure that eighth defender gets blocked too, by a player who arrives with a running start.

```{python}
#| label: fig-power-i
#| fig-cap: "The Power I's arithmetic: eight blockers for eight defenders in the box (the 4-3's seven plus the strong safety, SS, walked down outside the tight end). The run goes off right tackle. The right tackle blocks down on the tackle (T) inside him, the tight end (Y) turns the end (E) out, the right guard climbs to the Mike (M) and the left guard to the Will (W), who is chasing from the far side. The two lead backs (aqua rings) go through the hole first: the fullback (F) onto the Sam (S), the halfback (H) onto the safety. The tailback (R) follows them. Every defender near the ball has a blocker; the only free defenders are the deep safety (FS) and the cornerbacks (C)."
def power_i_play():
    off = players_of("Power I")
    dfn = base43(off, shell="single_high", fix={"SS": dict(d=5.0, w=8.6), "RCB": dict(d=6.5, w=11.5)})
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    p.path("SAM", [(2.6, 5.5)], absolute=True, delay=0.3)
    p.path("SS", [(3.4, 7.6)], absolute=True, delay=0.3)
    p.path("MIKE", [(3.4, 1.8)], absolute=True, delay=0.3)
    p.path("WILL", [(3.8, -0.4)], absolute=True, delay=0.3)
    p.block("LT", target="WDE")
    p.block("C", target="WDT")
    p.block("LG", target="WILL", speed=3.2)
    p.block("RG", target="MIKE", speed=3.2)
    p.block("RT", pts=[(1.1, -0.7)])                                 # down on the 3-technique
    p.block("Y", pts=[(1.2, 0.3)])                                   # turn the end out
    p.block("FB", pts=[(3.0, 2.9), (6.1, 4.6)], speed=6.0)           # through the hole onto the Sam
    p.block("HB", pts=[(3.0, 1.9), (6.9, 4.6)], speed=6.0)           # onto the safety
    p.path("QB", [(-3.0, 0.9)], absolute=True)
    p.run("RB", [(-3.6, 1.3), (0.0, 3.2), (5.0, 3.3), (9.5, 3.3)], absolute=True, delay=0.25)
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.8)
    p.highlight("FB", "HB", "RB", color=RB_RING)
    p.highlight("SS", color=style.DEFENSE)
    return p

pwr = power_i_play()
fld = pwr.draw(lateral=(-15.0, 17.0), window=(-9.0, 15.0), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(fld.ax)
label(fld, pwr, "two lead blockers:\nF on the Sam,\nH on the safety", (-5.4, 11.6), target=(-4.5, 2.1))
label(fld, pwr, "8 blockers vs 8 in the box", (9.0, -8.0))
plt.show()
```

The price is visible in the picture: one wide receiver. The defense, seeing three backs and one
receiver, can bring everyone near the line, and often does.

## Singleback and ace: trading the fullback for a tight end

Through the 1960s and '70s, defenses got better at stopping two-back formations, and in 1978 the NFL
changed its rules to help the passing game (pass blockers could extend their arms, and defenders
could contact receivers only within five yards of the line;[^rules78] [1978 and the Passing
Revolution](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd) has the story). Offenses wanted more
receivers on the field. The simplest place to find one was the backfield.

A [**singleback**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-singleback) formation keeps the quarterback under
center but uses only one running back, directly behind him, usually about seven yards deep. The
second back is gone: his spot on the field goes to a third receiver or a second tight end. With three
receivers it's 11 personnel, the NFL's most common grouping; with two tight ends it's 12.

The two-tight-end version has its own name. The [**ace formation**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-ace-formation)
is a singleback formation with a tight end on each side of the line and two wide receivers (12
personnel). (Some teams say "ace" for any one-back look; the broadcast usage is the two-tight-end one.)

```{python}
#| label: fig-singleback-ace
#| fig-cap: "The one-back family. Left: singleback with 11 personnel, a tight end (Y) on the right and three receivers (X on the line, H in the slot, Z off the line). Right: the ace, 12 personnel, a tight end on each side (Y and U) and both receivers a yard off the line, so the formation is the same on both sides. In both, the lone running back (R) is about seven yards deep, directly behind the quarterback, which lets him start toward either side."
fig, out = plate_pair("Singleback", "Ace")
plt.show()
```

### Why it exists: a tight end does a fullback's job, and more

Taking the fullback off the field sounds like giving up the lead blocker. The insight of the one-back
coaches was that a **tight end can do most of a fullback's job from a different spot**, and a lot
more besides. A tight end next to the tackle can block the same linebacker a fullback would have led
on, or he can run a pass route down the middle, which a fullback almost never does. A second tight
end on the other side makes the formation *balanced*: the same on both sides. A defense usually
sets its [strong side](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) to the tight end (its biggest
linebacker and a safety go there), but with a tight end on each side there isn't one, and the
offense can run either way with an extra blocker.

The lone back benefits too. Seven yards deep and directly behind the quarterback, he can start
toward either side and see the whole line. That's exactly what the zone running schemes of the 1990s
onward wanted, a back who reads the blocks and picks his hole, and it's why one-back, two-tight-end
sets became a main home of zone running, alongside the I ([Zone
Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd) draws it).

What did it give up? The fullback's head start. A tight end blocking from the line meets the
linebacker sooner, but with less of a running start, and the tailback no longer has a blocker leading
him into the hole. The ace's balance has a cost of its own, too: with a tight end on each side and the
receivers tight, it has only two wide receivers, so it can't stretch the coverage the way three-receiver
sets can. One-back offenses answered the lead-blocker problem with
[motion](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd): move a tight end or an off-the-line
"H-back" across the formation before the snap so that he ends up where the lead blocker is needed.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Washington, 1981–1992"}
Joe Gibbs, a Don Coryell assistant who became Washington's head coach in 1981, built the most
influential one-back offense in NFL history, and won three Super Bowls with it, after the 1982, 1987
and 1991 seasons, with three different starting quarterbacks (Joe Theismann, Doug Williams and Mark
Rypien).[^gibbs] The story Gibbs told was about one player: the Giants' Lawrence Taylor, a linebacker
so fast off the edge that a running back couldn't block him. Gibbs's answer was to take the second
back out of the backfield and put a second tight end, often a smaller, quicker one who lined up off
the line beside the tackle or went in motion (the *H-back*, a version of the [H, or move
player](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd)), where he could get his hands on Taylor before
Taylor got going.

The H-back became the one-back offense's Swiss army knife: he could block like a fullback, release
like a tight end, or move across the formation before the snap. Behind him, Washington's huge line (the
"Hogs") ran the plays that made the era famous, including the [counter
trey](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd), in which two linemen pulled the opposite way
from the backfield's first step.

**What to notice:** the H-back is a fullback and a tight end in one body, and he forces the defense
to decide which he is on every snap.
:::

Watch how one H-back changes the picture before the snap. The offense starts with both tight ends on
the right: Y on the line and the H-back (H) a step behind the right tackle. The defense sets its
strength there: its 3-technique tackle, its Sam linebacker and its strong safety go to the right.
Then the H-back moves.

```{python}
#| label: fig-hback-strip
#| fig-cap: "One-back motion (simulated, BDB-format tracking), zoomed on the box; the H-back (H) is ringed gold, the running back (R) aqua. 1: 12 personnel with both tight ends on the right, so the defense sets its strength there: the 3-technique tackle (T) and the Sam (S) are on the right. 2: H motions across behind the quarterback. The linebackers bump over a step but the defensive line doesn't move. 3: at the snap H is off the line outside the left tackle: now there's a tight end on each side, balanced like an ace, but the defense is still set to the right, so the left is where its strength isn't. 4: the run goes left. H blocks the end (E), the left tackle climbs to the Will (W), the left guard to the Mike (M), the center takes the 1-technique tackle, and R runs off H's block with a blocker for every defender on that side."
def hback_play():
    off = line5() + [QB, P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R"), Y, P("H", "TE", -2.4, 3.6),
                     P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -13.0), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 13.5)]
    dfn = base43(off, fix={"SAM": dict(d=4.0, w=6.6), "MIKE": dict(w=1.0), "WILL": dict(w=-2.8)})
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
    p.motion("H", pts=[(-1.0, -2.4), (0.0, -6.0), (0.8, -8.7), (0.8, -9.6)], speed=5.5)  # ends moving sideways
    p.motion("WILL", pts=[(0.0, -1.8)], speed=1.2)        # the linebackers bump a step toward the motion
    p.motion("MIKE", pts=[(0.0, -1.2)], speed=0.9)
    p.path("WILL", [(3.4, -4.6)], absolute=True, delay=0.3, speed=4.5)
    p.path("MIKE", [(3.6, -1.6)], absolute=True, delay=0.3, speed=4.5)
    p.path("WDE", [(1.5, -5.4)], absolute=True, delay=0.3, speed=1.6)
    p.path("WDT", [(1.4, 0.0)], absolute=True, delay=0.3, speed=1.4)
    p.block("H", target="WDE", speed=4.0)
    p.block("LT", target="WILL", speed=3.0, delay=0.1)
    p.block("LG", target="MIKE", speed=3.0, delay=0.1)
    p.block("C", target="WDT")
    p.path("QB", [(-2.8, -0.9)], absolute=True)
    p.run("RB", [(-4.8, -1.3), (-1.5, -3.2), (2.6, -3.4), (8.0, -3.6)], absolute=True, delay=0.25)
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.6)
    return p

animation_or_strip(hback_play(), [-2.0, -0.6, 0.0, 1.2], lateral=(-11.5, 11.5), window=(-8.5, 9.0),
                   rings=(("H", TE_RING), ("RB", RB_RING)),
                   notes=["both tight ends right; defense strong right", "H motions across; LBs bump, line stays",
                          "snap: a tight end each side, defense still right", "run left: H on the end, R behind him"])
```

After the motion the formation is balanced, like an ace, but the defense isn't: its line set to the
right and didn't flip, so the offense runs at the 1-technique side with a blocker it didn't have two
seconds ago. That front-against-formation mismatch is why the motion works. Most defenses bump their
linebackers a step, as here; some send the Sam across with the tight end, and then the H-back has to
block *him*. [Motion and Shifts as Weapons](02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd) tells the rest.

## The option branch: wishbone and flexbone

The other way to use the T's three backs is to keep all three and let the quarterback **choose who
gets the ball after the snap.** That's [option football](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd):
the offense leaves a defender unblocked on purpose, the quarterback reads what he does, and gives the
ball to whichever back the defender didn't take. Option football has its own chapter. Here we only
need the two formations it made famous.

```{python}
#| label: fig-option-plates
#| fig-cap: "The option formations. Left: the wishbone (31 personnel), a full house: the fullback (F) close behind the quarterback, and two halfbacks (H) a yard deeper and wider, behind the tackles, so the backs form an upside-down Y. Right: the flexbone (usually 30 personnel): one back (B) behind the quarterback, two slotbacks (A) standing a yard and a half off the line just outside the tackles, and two wide receivers (X and Z) both on the line, which makes the seven on the line legal without a tight end. A and B are the flexbone's own letters: A-backs and the B-back."
fig, out = plate_pair("Wishbone", "Flexbone")
plt.show()
```

### The wishbone

The [**wishbone**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wishbone) was drawn up at the University of Texas
in 1968 by offensive coordinator Emory Bellard, who moved the T's fullback up close behind the
quarterback and set the two halfbacks deeper and wider, one on each side. A Houston sportswriter,
Mickey Herskowitz, said it looked like a "pulley bone" (an old Southern name for a chicken's
wishbone), and head coach Darrell Royal turned that into "wishbone."[^bellard] Texas won 30 straight
games with it,
Oklahoma and Alabama adopted it, and through the 1970s the wishbone was the most feared offense in
college football.

The geometry is built for the [triple option](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd), the
play that gives the formation its purpose: three possible ball carriers, and the quarterback decides
who gets the ball by reading two unblocked defenders after the snap. The fullback, close to the line,
is the first threat (the "dive"), straight ahead. The quarterback is the second, running along the
line. The third is the halfback from the *other* side, who starts away from the play and sprints
across behind the quarterback as the pitch man; that's why the halfbacks line up deeper than the
fullback, so he has room to get across. The playside halfback leads around the edge and blocks the
defender who would tackle the pitch man. So every back has a job on every play, dive, lead or
pitch, toward either side; that is what a full house buys an option team. ([Option
Football](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd) draws the reads.)

### The flexbone

The wishbone's weakness was width. With all three backs bunched behind the quarterback and only one
receiver, defenses could crowd the line and outnumber the option. The
[**flexbone**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flexbone), which grew out of the wishbone in the
late 1970s and 1980s, takes the two halfbacks out of the deep backfield and stands them just off the line,
outside the tackles, as *slotbacks*. A fullback stays behind the quarterback, and there are two
wide receivers on the line, usually with no tight end. Who invented it is disputed: Bellard himself
(at Mississippi State in 1979), Fisher DeBerry's Air Force teams and Paul Johnson at Georgia Southern
all have a claim.[^flex]

Why there? A slotback just off the line is three things at once. He can *block* a defender on the
edge from a short distance. He can *go in motion* before the snap and arrive at the pitch man's
spot just as the ball is snapped, so the defense doesn't know which side the option is going. And he
can *run a pass route* immediately, because he's already past the line's congestion. The two
receivers outside force the defense to keep two defenders wide, which takes them out of the
[box](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd), the area near the ball where the run is defended (roughly
tight end to tight end, five to seven yards deep). The flexbone spreads the defense like a passing
formation while keeping three runners near the ball.

What does it give up against the wishbone? Inside power. With the halfbacks moved up to the edges,
the flexbone has no lead blocker lined up behind the quarterback for a run between the tackles, and
no tight end; it beats the defense with angles and width, not with bodies at the point of attack.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Navy and Georgia Tech, Paul Johnson's flexbone"}
No coach is more closely tied to the flexbone than Paul Johnson. He won two Division I-AA titles with it
at Georgia Southern (1999 and 2000), took over a Navy team that had gone 0–10 in 2001 and had it
winning eight games within two seasons, then ran the same offense against Atlantic Coast Conference
defenses at Georgia Tech from 2008 to 2018.[^johnson] Why would an undersized team choose an old
formation? Because it changes the problem. The service academies can't recruit 310-pound linemen; they
can recruit disciplined players who block quickly at defenders' legs and carry out fakes on every
play, and the flexbone makes the defense play assignment football for sixty minutes, something
defenses that see it once a year rarely practice. (Even Navy has since moved much of its option game
into the shotgun.[^navy])

**What to notice:** when you see a flexbone team on a Saturday, watch the slotbacks before the snap.
The one who goes in motion is usually telling you which way the option is headed, and the other
one is often a blocker.
:::

You won't see either formation in the NFL. Option football needs a quarterback who takes a hit on
most plays, and NFL teams won't spend their most expensive player that way; NFL defenders are also
fast enough to cover the width the option relies on. But the *idea*, a quarterback who reads a
defender instead of blocking him, came back to the NFL from the shotgun, as the [zone
read](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd): the quarterback reads one unblocked defender and
either hands off or keeps the ball himself. [The
College Laboratory](../11-history/11-03-the-college-laboratory.qmd) traces that lineage, from the
wishbone and veer to the spread option.

## The Wing-T: misdirection

The last classic branch crossed the T with its ancestor. Around 1950 Dave Nelson, at Maine and then
Delaware, combined the quick-hitting T backfield with the single wing's *wingback*, a back lined up
just outside and a yard behind the tight end.[^wingt] The
[**Wing-T**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wing-t) puts the quarterback under center, a fullback
directly behind him, a halfback beside the fullback on the side away from the tight end, and the
wingback outside the tight end on the other side, with a split end on the halfback's side. Counted as
backs, the wingback and halfback make it 31 personnel; teams that use a receiver at wingback call it
21.

```{python}
#| label: fig-wing-t
#| fig-cap: "The Wing-T's buck sweep series: one backfield action, four endings. The formation in every panel: fullback (F) directly behind the quarterback, halfback (H) behind the left tackle, wingback (W) just outside and behind the tight end (Y) on the right, split end (X) on the left. In each panel the bold green arrow is the back who gets the ball and the gray dashed arrows are the backs faking; for the first second all four plays look alike. 1: the fullback hits straight up the middle (the buck, or a trap). 2: the buck sweep: the halfback runs to the wing side behind both guards, who pull (dark blue). 3: the wingback comes back the other way on a counter while everyone else flows toward the sweep. 4: the waggle: the quarterback fakes to both backs, then rolls out the other way to run or throw."
WT_WIN, WT_LAT = (-8.2, 3.0), (-13.6, 13.6)
BUCK = [(-4.5, 0.0), (-2.6, 0.9), (1.4, 0.9)]
SWEEP = [(-4.5, -3.2), (-5.5, -1.0), (-5.3, 2.0), (-3.7, 6.0), (-0.6, 10.6)]
COUNTER = [(-1.5, 7.4), (-3.0, 4.0), (-3.3, -3.0), (-1.2, -8.2)]
WAGGLE = [(-1.9, 0.0), (-3.0, 0.7), (-5.8, -2.0), (-6.4, -7.6)]
SERIES = [("1. Buck: the fullback", BUCK, [SWEEP]),
          ("2. Buck sweep: the halfback", SWEEP, [BUCK]),
          ("3. Counter: the wingback", COUNTER, [BUCK, SWEEP]),
          ("4. Waggle: the quarterback", WAGGLE, [BUCK, SWEEP])]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.9))
for ax, (title, real, fakes) in zip(axes.flat, SERIES):
    p, fld = plate(ax, "Wing-T", sub=False, title=title, window=WT_WIN, lateral=WT_LAT)
    for f in fakes:
        threat(fld, p, f, color=FAKE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 2)))
    if real is SWEEP:      # both guards pull toward the wing side, in front of the quarterback
        for g0, dd, w1, end in [(1.6, -1.5, 5.6, (0.8, 8.4)), (-1.6, -1.5, 3.6, (0.4, 6.4))]:
            xs, ys = XY(fld, p, np.array([LINE_D, dd, dd, end[0]]), np.array([g0, g0 + 0.6, w1, end[1]]))
            ax.plot(xs[:-1], ys[:-1], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.6, zorder=9)
            ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=9,
                                         color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.6, zorder=9))
    threat(fld, p, real, color=THREAT, lw=2.1)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.94, bottom=0.13, wspace=0.05, hspace=0.24)
ring_legend(fig, extra=[Line2D([], [], color=THREAT, lw=2.1, ls=(0, (3, 2)), label="ball carrier"),
                        Line2D([], [], color=FAKE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 2)), label="a fake"),
                        Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.6, label="pulling guard")], ncol=3)
plt.show()
```

### Why it exists: making the defense guess

The Wing-T's purpose is [misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd):
making the defense commit to one direction and then going the other. With three backs placed so that
each can carry the ball in a different direction, and a quarterback who turns his back to the
defense and fakes to each of them in turn, every play looks the same for its first second. The
Wing-T is organized in [series](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd): groups of
plays that start with the same backfield action and end differently. The famous one is the [buck
sweep](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd) series in the figure. Its base play
is the sweep: the line blocks *down* (each blocker hits the defender inside him, from the side) while
both guards pull, running sideways behind the line to lead the halfback around the wing. When the
defense starts chasing the sweep, the same first second becomes the fullback's buck up the middle or a
[trap](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd) (a defensive lineman is let through
unblocked and then hit from the side by a pulling lineman), a wingback counter back the other way, or
the [waggle](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd), the Wing-T's bootleg: the
quarterback fakes, rolls out the other way behind a pulling guard and runs or throws. Defenders who
*flow* (run toward the side the play seems to be going) with the first thing they see get punished;
defenders who wait get blocked.

The trade is complexity and, again, width. A misdirection offense needs a lot of practice time to run
its fakes well, and its backs are runners and blockers, not receivers. You'll rarely see a true
Wing-T on Sunday, but you'll see its children every week: the jet sweep, in which a receiver sprints
across behind the line just as the ball is snapped, the down-block-and-pull schemes of the NFL's
[gap runs](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd), and the NFL bootleg are Wing-T ideas in
an NFL uniform ([Perimeter Runs and
Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd) traces them).

## The goal-line formation: everyone in close

Near the goal line the field gets short and narrow at the same time. There's no room behind the
defense to throw deep, and the offense needs a yard or two, not twenty. So every team keeps a
[**goal-line formation**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-goal-line-formation): the quarterback
under center, two backs stacked behind him, three tight ends (or a sixth lineman, the
[jumbo](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd) grouping), and no wide receivers at all. Everyone lines up
tight to the ball. In personnel terms that's 23, or 14 with a tight end standing at fullback, or a
jumbo grouping.

```{python}
#| label: fig-goal-line
```
