```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-goal at the 1: the goal-line formation (23 personnel) against a goal-line defense (five linemen, three linebackers, three defensive backs). Offense: three tight ends (Y and U on the line, H a wing just behind and outside Y), a fullback (F) and a tailback (R), with the linemen's splits narrowed to about a yard and a quarter. Defense: the linemen (E = end, T = tackle, N = nose) crowd the ball in the gaps, the linebackers (S/M/W) stand about two yards off it, and even the cornerback (C) and safeties (SS, FS) are within five yards. Count: nine blockers against eleven defenders, every one of them in the box."
gl_def = [D("LE", "DE", 0.5, -4.65, "E"), D("DLT", "DT", 0.5, -1.9, "T"), D("NT", "NT", 0.5, 0.0, "N"),
          D("DRT", "DT", 0.5, 1.9, "T"), D("RE", "DE", 0.5, 4.6, "E"),
          D("WILL", "WILL", 2.0, -3.3, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 2.0, 0.8, "M"), D("SAM", "SAM", 1.8, 6.6, "S"),
          D("LCB", "CB", 1.8, -6.6, "C"), D("SS", "SS", 4.2, 4.0), D("FS", "FS", 4.6, -2.4)]
p = ring_by_body(Play(players_of("Goal line"), gl_def, los=109, to_go=None))
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-13.0, 13.0), window=(-9.0, 8.5), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(fld.ax)
label(fld, p, "9 blockers: 5 linemen,\n3 tight ends, fullback", (-5.6, -8.3))
label(fld, p, "11 defenders,\nall in the box", (6.6, -8.9))
for i, w in enumerate([-4.55, -3.2, -1.9, -0.62, 0.62, 1.9, 3.2, 4.55, 6.3]):   # the nine gaps
    x, y = XY(fld, p, -3.15, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, str(i + 1), fontsize=6.4, ha="center", va="center", color=style.INK_2, zorder=12,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.5))
label(fld, p, "nine gaps to fill\n(numbered below them)", (-5.6, 8.4))
plt.show()
```

### Why it exists: shrink the field, pick the spot

Do the count from the iso. The offense has nine blockers: five linemen, three tight ends and the
fullback (the quarterback and the tailback don't block). The defense has eleven players, and at the
goal line all eleven are in the box, because there's no deep field left to protect. Eleven against
nine: on paper the defense wins the count by two, and down here it always will. So the goal-line
formation isn't trying to win the count. It's trying to make the count matter less, in two ways.

First, it **shrinks the space**. Runs are aimed at [gaps](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd),
the spaces between blockers, and every defender near the ball is assigned one to fill. Tight splits
(here about a yard and a quarter between linemen, against the usual yard and a half or more) and
everyone close to the ball leave narrow gaps with little room to slip through. Count them in the
figure: the seven players on the line make eight gaps, and the wing makes a ninth. The defense needs a
player in each of the nine before it has anyone left over. Second, the offense **picks the spot**. It
needs one yard, not ten, so it can pour extra bodies into a single gap: a double team on the line, the
fullback leading into the hole, and a tailback who only has to fall forward. The defense's two spare
players are somewhere on a crowded line, and they may never reach the one gap that matters. The defense
answers by bringing its own heavy package and crowding the line, so the goal line is the one place in
football where both sides deliberately give up all their space.

The price is that a defense that knows you'll run can commit everyone to stopping it. That's why the
goal-line formation is also where a lot of short play-action touchdowns come from: the quarterback
fakes the handoff, every defender bites, and one of the three tight ends, who looked like a blocker,
slips into the end zone alone. In 2022–2025, about three of every four NFL plays inside the 2-yard line
that came from under center with two or more backs were runs; when they were passes, about four in
five used a play fake.[^gl] (The [quarterback sneak](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd)
starts here too, and so does its push-assisted version, the [tush
push](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd), in which teammates
shove the quarterback forward from behind, still legal in 2026.) [Red Zone, Goal Line, and Short
Yardage](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd) is where that
fight gets its full treatment.

## Matching formations to personnel

Personnel comes first, so the formation is usually a short list once you've counted the backs and
tight ends. The table below is the cheat sheet. The pairings are typical, not laws: a team can line
up 21 personnel in the shotgun, or 12 personnel in an I with a tight end at fullback.

| Formation | Typical personnel | Backfield | Built for | Where you'll see it now |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T-formation | 32 | Three backs side by side | Quick hitting runs to either side | Goal line (as a full house), rarely |
| Pro set (split backs) | 21 | Two backs side by side | Balance: run either way, backs in the flats | Occasionally, mostly play-action |
| I-formation | 21 (or 22) | Two backs stacked | Lead blocker, downhill tailback | 21-personnel teams; short yardage |
| Offset I | 21 (or 22) | Fullback a yard or two to one side | Better angles for the lead block | Same as the I |
| Power I | 31 | I plus a halfback | Two lead blockers | Goal line and short yardage |
| Singleback | 11 | One back at ~7 yards | Three receivers with an under-center run game | Every NFL team, every week |
| Ace | 12 | One back at ~7 yards | Balance, a tight end blocker on both sides | Every NFL team, every week |
| Wishbone | 31 (or 32) | Fullback close, halfbacks deep and wide | The triple option | History, some high schools |
| Flexbone | 30 | One back, two slotbacks | Option with width | Service academies, high schools |
| Wing-T | 31 (or 21) | Fullback, halfback, wingback | Misdirection, series football | High school; its ideas in the NFL |
| Goal-line | 23 (or 14, or jumbo) | Two backs stacked | Narrow gaps, extra blockers at one spot | Every NFL team, inside the 3 |

And the reverse direction, from what you count to what you should expect:

- **One back, quarterback under center:** singleback (11) or ace (12).
- **Two backs, quarterback under center:** I, offset I or pro set (21 or 22). Look at whether they're
  stacked, offset or side by side.
- **Three backs:** Power I, wishbone or T (31 or 32), almost always short yardage in the NFL.
- **No wide receivers and three tight ends:** goal-line.
- **Quarterback in the shotgun:** you're in [the next chapter's](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd)
  world, even with two backs.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
**"Formation names are universal."** They're universal enough for broadcasts, but not in
playbooks. One team's "ace" is another's "Deuce" or "Tiger"; Lombardi called split backs "Red," and
other systems call two-back looks "Near," "Far" and "Split." Even the broadcast names blur: an offset I
with a tight end at fullback, or a one-back set with the quarterback in the pistol, may be called three
different things by three analysts. Learn the shapes, not just the words: under center or not, how many backs, where they
stand, where the tight ends are. The shape is what tells the defense, and you, what's possible.
:::

## Why the classic formations faded

For most of the twentieth century, the quarterback took the snap under center on nearly every play.
Today he does it on about a third of them. Here's what that decline looks like in the data.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (load play-by-play 2006-2025 and FTN charting 2022-2025)"
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

COLS = ["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "posteam", "down", "ydstogo", "yardline_100",
        "play_type", "pass", "shotgun", "wp", "half_seconds_remaining", "epa"]
plays = pbp(range(2006, 2026), columns=COLS)
plays = plays[(plays.season_type == "REG") & plays.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"]) & plays.down.notna()].copy()

ftn = nfl().load_ftn_charting([2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]).to_pandas()
ftn["qb_loc"] = ftn["qb_location"].astype(str).str.strip()
ftn = ftn[["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id", "qb_loc", "n_offense_backfield", "is_play_action"]]
recent = plays[plays.season >= 2022].merge(ftn, how="left", left_on=["game_id", "play_id"],
                                            right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id"])
recent["two_back"] = recent["n_offense_backfield"] >= 2     # two or more players in the backfield besides the QB
recent["neutral"] = (recent.down.isin([1, 2]) & recent.wp.between(0.2, 0.8)
                     & (recent.half_seconds_remaining > 120))
print(f"{len(plays):,} regular-season runs and passes 2006-2025; {len(recent):,} of them 2022-2025")

# reason 1: EPA per dropback (pass = 1 includes sacks and scrambles) vs per designed run
epa_pass = plays[plays["pass"] == 1].groupby("season")["epa"].mean()
epa_run = plays[plays["pass"] == 0].groupby("season")["epa"].mean()
assert 0.02 < epa_pass[2025] < 0.07 and -0.07 < epa_run[2025] < -0.02
assert (epa_pass - epa_run).min() > 0      # dropbacks out-gained runs on average in every season

# neutral-situation pass rates by backfield (quoted under "What the I gives up")
nt = recent[recent.neutral]
uc2 = nt[(nt.qb_loc == "U") & (nt.n_offense_backfield >= 2)]
uc1 = nt[(nt.qb_loc == "U") & (nt.n_offense_backfield == 1)]
gun01 = nt[(nt.qb_loc == "S") & (nt.n_offense_backfield <= 1)]
pa = lambda x: x[x["pass"] == 1].is_play_action.astype(float).mean() * 100   # noqa: E731
assert 0.25 < uc2["pass"].mean() < 0.30 and 0.35 < uc1["pass"].mean() < 0.41 and 75 < pa(uc1) < 82
assert 0.68 < gun01["pass"].mean() < 0.74 and 82 < pa(uc2) < 88
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-shotgun-trend
#| fig-cap: "The quarterback moves back. Left: share of NFL regular-season runs and passes snapped to a quarterback in the shotgun, 2006–2025 (nflverse play-by-play `shotgun` flag; the rest are under center or, in recent seasons, a few percent from the pistol). Right: where the quarterback lined up, 2022–2025, from FTN's play-by-play charting (which records under center, shotgun and pistol separately). The shotgun peaked in 2023 and fell back in 2025, when under center rose to about a third of plays. Different sources, so different panels."
gun = plays.groupby("season")["shotgun"].mean() * 100
loc = (recent.assign(U=recent.qb_loc == "U", P=recent.qb_loc == "P", S=recent.qb_loc == "S")
       .groupby("season")[["U", "P", "S"]].mean() * 100)

fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.1), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[2.1, 1]))
a1.plot(gun.index, gun.values, color=style.OFFENSE, marker="o", ms=3.2, lw=2.2)
a1.plot(gun.index, 100 - gun.values, color=style.DEFENSE, marker="o", ms=3.2, lw=2.2)
a1.text(2025.3, gun.loc[2025], f"shotgun\n{gun.loc[2025]:.0f}%", va="center", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK)
a1.text(2025.3, 100 - gun.loc[2025], f"not shotgun\n{100 - gun.loc[2025]:.0f}%", va="center", fontsize=7.5,
        color=style.INK)
a1.text(2006, gun.loc[2006] - 6.5, f"{gun.loc[2006]:.0f}%", ha="center", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK_2)
a1.text(2006, 100 - gun.loc[2006] + 3.5, f"{100 - gun.loc[2006]:.0f}%", ha="center", fontsize=7.5,
        color=style.INK_2)
a1.set_xlim(2005.2, 2028.6)
a1.set_xticks([2006, 2010, 2014, 2018, 2022, 2025], ["2006", "2010", "2014", "2018", "2022", "2025"], fontsize=8)
a1.set_ylim(0, 100)
a1.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=8)
a1.set_ylabel("share of plays (%)", fontsize=8)
a1.set_title("Shotgun vs not, 2006–2025 (pbp)", fontsize=9.5)

cols = {"U": style.DEFENSE, "P": style.THIRD, "S": style.OFFENSE}
names = {"U": "under center", "P": "pistol", "S": "shotgun"}
bottom = np.zeros(len(loc))
for k in ["U", "P", "S"]:
    a2.bar(loc.index, loc[k], bottom=bottom, color=cols[k], width=0.7, edgecolor=style.SURFACE, label=names[k])
    for x, b, v in zip(loc.index, bottom, loc[k]):
        if v >= 7:
            a2.text(x, b + v / 2, f"{v:.0f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.2, color="white")
    bottom += loc[k].values
a2.set_xticks(loc.index, [f"'{y % 100:02d}" for y in loc.index], fontsize=8)
a2.set_ylim(0, 100)
a2.set_yticks([])
a2.grid(False)
a2.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
a2.set_title("QB location (FTN)", fontsize=9.5)
a2.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.1), ncol=2, fontsize=7, frameon=False, handlelength=1.0,
          columnspacing=0.8)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
# guard the numbers quoted in the text against a data refresh
assert 15 < gun.loc[2006] < 25 and 68 < gun.loc[2023] < 75 and 62 < gun.loc[2025] < 70, gun
assert 30 < loc.loc[2025, "U"] < 37 and 25 < loc.loc[2023, "U"] < 30, loc
```

In 2006 offenses were in the shotgun on about one play in five. By 2023 it was about 72%. Over the same
years the I-formation's share of plays fell from about 11% in 2016 to about 6% in 2022, as far as the
formation labels in the public data go.[^ngsform] The causes overlap, but there are five worth
knowing.

1. **Passing became more valuable than running.** After the 1978 rule changes, and again as
   offenses learned to throw efficiently, a pass gained more on average than a run. In the
   [EPA](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd) terms you met in Downs,
   Distance, and Field Position, NFL dropbacks (sacks and scrambles included) averaged about +0.04
   expected points per play in 2025 and designed runs about −0.05; across 2006–2025 it was about +0.03
   against −0.07, and dropbacks came out ahead in every one of those seasons.[^epa] [Expected Points and Success
   Rate](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd) shows how analysts
   measure that gap, and why it's smaller than it looks (runs are less risky, and they set up the
   pass). An offense that passes more wants more receivers, and the second back is the first player to
   go.
2. **The shotgun is a better place to pass from.** Five yards back, the quarterback takes a shorter
   drop and never has to turn his back on the defense. He sees the coverage from the snap and has
   more time before the rush arrives. The shotgun was used in the NFL as early as 1960
   and revived by Tom Landry's Cowboys in 1975, but for decades it was a third-down formation;[^gun]
   [the history chapters](../11-history/11-01-single-wing-to-scoring-drought.qmd) follow it.
3. **Spreading the defense makes running easier, too.** Three or four receivers pull defensive
   backs out wide, which leaves fewer defenders near the ball. An offense in the shotgun with 11
   personnel can often run against six defenders in the box instead of seven or eight: the same
   count you did for the iso, now tilted toward the offense. Spread formations are [the next chapter](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd).
4. **College stopped producing under-center quarterbacks.** By the 2010s most college offenses, and
   many high schools, played almost entirely from the shotgun. Quarterbacks arrived in the NFL having
   rarely taken a snap under center, and NFL coaches built around what their quarterbacks did best.
5. **A fullback is an expensive specialist.** A roster spot used on a lead blocker is one not used on
   a receiver or tight end who can play every down. Many NFL teams stopped carrying a true fullback at
   all.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
**The shotgun won the passing game; the classic formations kept the running game's advantages.**
Under center, the quarterback can hand off to a back already running downhill, toward the line, and
fake a handoff with his back to the defense. In the shotgun, many runs start sideways, and a play fake
is less convincing because the defense can see the ball the whole time. Each formation is a bundle of
trade-offs, and the NFL's long move to the shotgun traded the run game's angles for the passing
game's vision. The 2025 turn back toward under center is offenses deciding they gave up too much.
:::

## Where the classic formations survive

The I-formation isn't dead. It has retreated to the places where its advantages matter most, and in
2025 it started coming back out. Look at what lining up under center tells you now:

```{python}
#| label: fig-under-center-today
#| fig-cap: "What lining up under center means in the 2025 NFL (regular season, FTN charting via nflverse). Left: how often the offense passed from each quarterback location. Middle: of the dropbacks from each location, the share that used a play-action fake. Right: the share of plays snapped under center, overall and on short yardage (1 yard or less to go) and inside the opponent's 2-yard line. Under center is a running alignment, it is the home of play-action, and it is the default when the offense needs a yard."
s = recent[recent.season == 2025]
locs = [("U", "under\ncenter"), ("P", "pistol"), ("S", "shotgun")]
pass_rate = [s[s.qb_loc == k]["pass"].mean() * 100 for k, _ in locs]
drop = s[s["pass"] == 1]
pa_rate = [drop[drop.qb_loc == k]["is_play_action"].astype(float).mean() * 100 for k, _ in locs]
uc = lambda x: (x.qb_loc == "U").mean() * 100   # noqa: E731
situ = [("all plays", uc(s)), ("1 yard or\nless to go", uc(s[s.ydstogo <= 1])),
        ("inside the\nopp. 2", uc(s[s.yardline_100 <= 2]))]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 2.7))
colors = [style.DEFENSE, style.THIRD, style.OFFENSE]
for ax, vals, title in [(axes[0], pass_rate, "Pass rate"), (axes[1], pa_rate, "Play-action share\nof dropbacks")]:
    ax.bar(range(3), vals, color=colors, width=0.62)
    for i, v in enumerate(vals):
        ax.text(i, v + 2, f"{v:.0f}%", ha="center", fontsize=8, color=style.INK)
    ax.set_xticks(range(3), [n for _, n in locs], fontsize=7.5)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9)
axes[2].bar(range(3), [v for _, v in situ], color=[style.MUTED, style.DEFENSE, style.DEFENSE], width=0.62)
for i, (_, v) in enumerate(situ):
    axes[2].text(i, v + 2, f"{v:.0f}%", ha="center", fontsize=8, color=style.INK)
axes[2].set_xticks(range(3), [n for n, _ in situ], fontsize=7.5)
axes[2].set_title("Snapped under center", fontsize=9)
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_ylim(0, 100)
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.grid(False)
    ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.2)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
assert 25 < pass_rate[0] < 36 and 75 < pass_rate[2] < 82 and 75 < pa_rate[0] < 88 and pa_rate[2] < 14, (pass_rate, pa_rate)
assert 55 < situ[1][1] < 70 and 30 < situ[0][1] < 37, situ
assert 25 < pass_rate[1] < 33 and 45 < pa_rate[1] < 56, (pass_rate, pa_rate)     # the pistol
# EPA per dropback by QB location, 2024-2025 (quoted in the revival section)
db = recent[(recent.season >= 2024) & (recent["pass"] == 1)]
epa_uc, epa_gun = db[db.qb_loc == "U"].epa.mean(), db[db.qb_loc == "S"].epa.mean()
assert 0.10 < epa_uc < 0.17 and 0.0 < epa_gun < 0.05, (epa_uc, epa_gun)
```

Three things stand out, and they're where the classic formations live now: two situations (short
yardage and play-action) and one kind of team (the few that still build around a fullback).

**Short yardage.** With a yard or less to go, NFL offenses lined up under center on about 63% of
plays in 2025, nearly twice their overall rate. When the offense needs one yard, the quick snap, the
downhill handoff and the extra blockers of the I and the goal-line formation are worth more than the
quarterback's view of the coverage. (The sneak and the tush push start from under center too.)

**Play-action.** About four of every five dropbacks from under center in 2025 used a play fake,
against about one in ten from the shotgun. That's no coincidence. A quarterback who turns his back to
the defense and puts the ball in a running back's belly is selling the run with his whole body, and
a two-back formation that usually runs is the best advertisement for a fake. The formation's
predictability is the bait. [Play-Action, Bootlegs, and
Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd) shows what the fake does to the
defense.

Notice the middle bar in each panel, too. The [pistol](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd)
isn't under center, so the next chapter files it with the shotgun, but in 2025 it behaved like a
cousin of this chapter's formations: offenses passed on only about 29% of pistol snaps, and about half
of those dropbacks used a play fake. That's what you'd expect from an alignment built to keep the
running back directly behind the quarterback: a downhill run and a believable fake, from a few yards
back.

**21 personnel.** A few NFL teams still build around a fullback, and they're among the most
interesting offenses in the league.

```{python}
#| label: fig-team-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Who still plays classic football: each NFL team's 2025 share of plays snapped under center (across) against its share with two or more players in the backfield besides the quarterback, usually two backs (up). Dashed lines are the league rates. The Rams, Seahawks and Bills led the under-center revival; the Dolphins, Ravens, Seahawks, Bills, Patriots and 49ers used the most two-back sets. Regular season, runs and passes; FTN charting via nflverse."
t = (recent[recent.season == 2025].groupby("posteam")
     .agg(uc=("qb_loc", lambda x: (x == "U").mean() * 100), two=("two_back", lambda x: x.mean() * 100)))
lg = recent[recent.season == 2025]
lg_uc, lg_two = (lg.qb_loc == "U").mean() * 100, lg.two_back.mean() * 100
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.9))
hot = {"LA": "Rams", "SEA": "Seahawks", "BUF": "Bills", "SF": "49ers", "BAL": "Ravens", "MIA": "Dolphins",
       "NE": "Patriots", "WAS": "Commanders", "KC": "Chiefs", "CIN": "Bengals", "DET": "Lions", "PHI": "Eagles"}
ax.scatter(t.uc, t.two, s=[34 if k in hot else 18 for k in t.index],
           color=[style.OFFENSE if k in hot else style.BASELINE for k in t.index], zorder=3,
           edgecolor="white", lw=0.6)
OFFS = {"LA": (-0.8, 0.0, "right"), "SEA": (0.0, 1.2, "center"), "BUF": (0.0, -1.3, "center"),
        "SF": (-1.4, 0.0, "right"), "BAL": (0.9, 0.0, "left"), "MIA": (-0.9, 0.0, "right"),
        "NE": (0.0, 1.2, "center"), "WAS": (0.0, 1.0, "center"), "KC": (0.9, 0.0, "left"),
        "CIN": (0.0, -1.1, "center"), "DET": (0.9, 0.0, "left"), "PHI": (0.9, 0.0, "left")}
for k, name in hot.items():
    dx, dy, ha = OFFS[k]
    ax.text(t.loc[k, "uc"] + dx, t.loc[k, "two"] + dy, name, fontsize=7.5, ha=ha, va="center", color=style.INK)
ax.axvline(lg_uc, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=1)
ax.axhline(lg_two, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=1)
ax.text(lg_uc + 0.4, 34.6, f"league {lg_uc:.0f}%", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, va="top")
ax.text(63.5, lg_two + 0.5, f"league {lg_two:.0f}%", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, ha="right", va="bottom")
ax.set_xlim(4, 64)
ax.set_ylim(8, 35)
ax.set_xlabel("snapped under center (% of plays)", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("two or more backs (% of plays)", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
ax.set_title("Under center and two-back usage by team, 2025", fontsize=10)
plt.show()
```

The two axes don't always go together, which is the interesting part. The Rams were the league's
most under-center team in 2025 (about 59% of plays) but used two backs only a little more than
average; their under-center snaps were mostly one-back looks with two or three tight ends. The
Dolphins were the opposite: more two-back plays than anyone, mostly from the shotgun and pistol. The
teams in the top right, the Seahawks, Bills, 49ers and Patriots, with the Ravens just over the
under-center line, are the ones still playing something close to classic football, a fullback and a tailback behind a quarterback under center, on a quarter of their
snaps or more.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: San Francisco 49ers, 2017–2025"}
Kyle Shanahan's 49ers have been the NFL's leading 21-personnel team for most of his tenure, with
fullback Kyle Juszczyk ([Personnel](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd) has the numbers). Much of it comes
from the I and offset I: Juszczyk lines up behind the quarterback, leads on a linebacker or the edge
defender on running plays, and on play-action slips out into the flat as the defense crashes on the
run. In 2025
the 49ers were under center on about 46% of plays, well above the league's 34%, and had two backs on
the field on about a quarter.[^niners]

The 49ers' version of the I isn't the 1970s version, though. Juszczyk motions out of the backfield,
lines up as a wing or in the slot, and returns to the I on the next play, so the defense can't key on
where he stands. The formation is classic; the way it's used is modern.

**What to notice:** when the 49ers line up in the I, watch where the fullback's path *ends*. His first
steps are designed to look the same on the run and on the fake. If he hits someone, it's a run; if he
crosses the formation as if to block the backside end, brushes past him and keeps going to the flat,
it's the bootleg, and the defense has been fooled by its own expectations.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Baltimore Ravens 2024, Patrick Ricard and Derrick Henry"}
The 2024 Ravens (head coach John Harbaugh, offensive coordinator Todd Monken, an era that ended after
2025) paired Lamar Jackson with Derrick Henry, who ran for 1,921 yards, second in the league, behind
Patrick Ricard, an undrafted defensive tackle from Maine turned 300-pound fullback.[^ravens] Baltimore had
two or more backs on the field on about a quarter of its 2024 plays, against a league rate of about
18%. A defense built to stop Jackson's passing sits in nickel; the Ravens line up with two backs, and
the nickel back suddenly has a 300-pound fullback coming at him. If the defense answers with
linebackers, Jackson throws over them: the [personnel](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd) dilemma, delivered
from a formation that has been around since the 1950s.

**What to notice:** in a classic two-back formation, find the fullback and do the count: blockers
against defenders in the box. If the defense matched the count with a defensive back where a
linebacker should be, the offense has the matchup it wanted; if it matched it with a linebacker, look
for the throw over him.
:::

### The 2025 under-center revival

The shotgun's share fell from 72% in 2023 to 66% in 2025, and FTN's charting has offenses under center
on 33.6% of plays in 2025, up from 27.3% in 2023.[^revival] The reason is the same arms race that sent
personnel heavier ([Personnel](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd) told that half): defenses spent the
early 2020s getting lighter and playing more two-deep safety looks to stop the pass, which left fewer
big bodies near the line. Offenses answered by getting bigger and putting the quarterback back under
center, where the run game has its best angles and play-action its best disguise. The offensive
side of the ledger pushed the same way. Wide zone and play-action from under center, the Shanahan and
McVay style, kept producing: in 2024 and 2025, dropbacks from under center averaged about +0.14
expected points per play against about +0.03 from the shotgun.[^ucepa] (That gap flatters under
center, whose passes come on downs when the defense is braced for a run, but that is exactly the
point of the formation.) And the quarterbacks who run those offenses are comfortable under center.
Sean McVay's Rams
were under center on about 59% of their 2025 snaps, the most in the league, and their quarterback,
Matthew Stafford, was the league's MVP. The champion Seahawks, under offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak
in 2025, were second, at about 53%.

Whether the turn lasts depends on the defense's answer, and in 2025 defenses were already answering by
playing more base. The old formations didn't come back because they were old. They came back because,
for now, they're the right answer to what defenses are doing. That's the pattern of this entire book.

## The classic formations on one page

Here are all eleven, reduced to what you'll actually see on a broadcast: the line, the quarterback
and the backfield. The backfield is the fingerprint, so it's what to memorize.

```{python}
#| label: fig-backfield-sheet
#| fig-cap: "The eleven classic backfields, with the shotgun for comparison (last panel). Only the players within about eight yards of the ball are shown: the line, the quarterback (Q), the backs (aqua rings) and any tight ends or wings (gold rings). Read them back to front: under center or not, how many backs, stacked, side by side or offset. Two spots look identical here and differ only in who stands there: the Wing-T's wingback (W, a running back) and the goal-line set's wing (H, a tight end). On a broadcast the picture can't tell you which; the personnel can."
names = ["T-formation", "Pro set", "I-formation", "Offset I", "Power I", "Singleback", "Ace", "Wishbone",
         "Flexbone", "Wing-T", "Goal line"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 4, figsize=(6.6, 4.2))
for ax, name in zip(axes.flat, names + ["Shotgun"]):
    pl = SHOTGUN if name == "Shotgun" else players_of(name)
    pl = [q for q in pl if abs(q.w) <= 8.0]
    p = ring_by_body(Play(pl, None, los=35, to_go=None))
    p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-8.6, 8.6), window=(-8.6, 1.6), title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    sub = "11 · gun" if name == "Shotgun" else FORMS[name][0]
    ax.set_title(f"{name}  ({sub})", fontsize=7.6, color=style.INK, loc="left", pad=2)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.95, bottom=0.01, hspace=0.32, wspace=0.06)
plt.show()
```

### What the backfield looks like on TV

Every diagram in this chapter is drawn from above, the way coaches draw them and the way the
[All-22](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd) film shows them. The broadcast mostly
isn't. The main [sideline camera](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd) sits high on
one side of the field, looking across it, so the direction the offense is moving runs left to right
across your screen and the width of the field is squashed into the up-down direction. That flips the
picture in a way worth knowing before you try to name a backfield live.

```{python}
#| label: fig-tv-view
#| fig-cap: "The same backfields as the broadcast's sideline camera sees them (a simple perspective sketch: camera high on the offense's left sideline, near the line of scrimmage, offense moving left to right; bodies are drawn as plain columns). The offensive line, which runs across the field, is squashed into a column at the right of each panel. Left: the I-formation. The stacked backs, one directly behind another from above, become a row strung out across the screen: quarterback, fullback, tailback, each farther from the line. Right: the pro set. The side-by-side backs are at the same depth, so they stand at the same spot left to right, one nearer the camera (lower on the screen and bigger) and one farther (higher and smaller), and they can hide behind each other. From the sideline, an I looks like a row and split backs look like a stack."
CAM = np.array([-1.0, -52.0, 24.0])      # (d, w, height) in yards: high on the offense's left sideline
LOOK = np.array([-2.5, 0.0, 0.0])


def tv_project(pts):
    """Pinhole projection of (d, w, z) points onto the camera's screen; returns screen (x, y), depth."""
    f = LOOK - CAM
    f /= np.linalg.norm(f)
    r = np.cross(f, [0.0, 0.0, 1.0])
    r /= np.linalg.norm(r)
    u = np.cross(r, f)
    v = np.atleast_2d(pts) - CAM
    depth = v @ f
    return np.c_[(v @ r) / depth, (v @ u) / depth], depth


def tv_panel(ax, name):
    pl = [q for q in players_of(name) if abs(q.w) <= 9.0]
    for d in range(-15, 11, 5):                      # yard lines, and the line of scrimmage
        xy, _ = tv_project(np.array([[d, -20.0, 0.0], [d, 20.0, 0.0]]))
        ax.plot(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8, zorder=1)
    xy, _ = tv_project(np.array([[0.0, -20.0, 0.0], [0.0, 20.0, 0.0]]))
    ax.plot(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.2, zorder=1)
    cols = []
    for q in pl:
        foot, dep = tv_project(np.array([q.d, q.w, 0.0]))
        head, _ = tv_project(np.array([q.d, q.w, 2.0]))
        cols.append((dep[0], q, foot[0], head[0]))
    for dep, q, foot, head in sorted(cols, key=lambda c: -c[0]):      # far players first
        wid = 0.75 * (head[1] - foot[1]) / 2.0
        ring = RB_RING if q.pos in ("RB", "FB") else TE_RING if q.pos == "TE" else "white"
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((foot[0] - wid / 2, foot[1]), wid, head[1] - foot[1],
                                    boxstyle=f"round,pad=0,rounding_size={wid * 0.45}", fc=style.OFFENSE,
                                    ec=ring, lw=1.8 if ring != "white" else 0.6, zorder=3))
        if q.label:
            ax.text(foot[0], foot[1] + 0.62 * (head[1] - foot[1]), q.label, ha="center", va="center",
                    fontsize=6.5, color="white", fontweight="bold", zorder=4)
    ax.set_facecolor(style.TURF)
    xs = [c[2][0] for c in cols]
    ys = [c[2][1] for c in cols] + [c[3][1] for c in cols]
    return (min(xs), max(xs), min(ys), max(ys))


def tv_frame(ax, ext, title):
    x0, x1, y0, y1 = ext
    padx, pady = 0.12 * (x1 - x0), 0.25 * (y1 - y0)
    ax.set_xlim(x0 - padx, x1 + padx)
    ax.set_ylim(y0 - pady, y1 + pady)
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
    for sp in ax.spines.values():
        sp.set_visible(False)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, loc="left")


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 2.4))
exts = [tv_panel(ax, n) for ax, n in zip(axes, ["I-formation", "Pro set"])]
ext = (min(e[0] for e in exts), max(e[1] for e in exts), min(e[2] for e in exts), max(e[3] for e in exts))
for ax, t in zip(axes, ["I-formation: a row", "Pro set: a stack"]):
    tv_frame(ax, ext, t)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.88, bottom=0.03, wspace=0.05)
plt.show()
```

So on the live shot, a row of helmets behind the quarterback is an I, one helmet seven yards back is
a singleback, and two backs stacked one above the other on screen are split backs. An offset fullback
is the second helmet sitting a little above or below the tailback's. The end-zone replay or the
skycam behind the offense shows the backfield the way this chapter draws it; use it to check your
call.

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: name that formation"}
For ten snaps in a row, before the ball is snapped, say three things out loud and then a name.

- **Under center or gun?** Look at the quarterback's hands. Under center means this chapter's
  formations; pistol or shotgun means [the next chapter's](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd).
- **One back or two (or three)?** Count the players strung out behind the quarterback (on the
  sideline camera, a row is an I and a stack is split backs). Name the shape by where they stand: a
  tight end directly behind the quarterback still makes it an I. A tight end off the line beside a
  tackle (an H-back) is a tight end for the personnel count.
- **Stacked, split or offset?** Two backs in a line is an I; side by side is a pro set; one a yard to
  the side is an offset I. Three backs is a Power I, a wishbone or a T, and in the NFL that means short
  yardage.
- **Where are the tight ends?** One on each side with one back is an ace. Three tight ends and no
  receivers is goal line.
- **Count.** Blockers (linemen, tight ends and any back who isn't getting the ball) against the
  defenders in the box. One more defender than blockers says the defense is braced for the run.
- **Name it, then guess.** Under center with two backs: lean run (about three plays in four), and if
  it's a pass, expect a play fake. Under center with one back: still run-leaning (about three passes
  in eight in neutral situations) and still play-action heavy. Note which way an offset fullback points
  and whether the play went that way.
- **Log it.** Add a formation column to your [prediction
  log](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd) next to personnel: "21, I, UC" or "12, ace,
  UC." After ten snaps, check how often your run/pass guess was right from under center versus from the
  gun.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: the offset fullback"}
Second-and-4 at your own 40, first quarter, tied. The offense has come out like this against a base
4-3:

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-offset
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: second-and-4. Offense: tight end Y (gold ring) on the right, backs ringed aqua, receivers X and Z. Defense: E = end, T = tackle, S/M/W = linebackers, C = cornerbacks, FS/SS = safeties."
off = players_of("Offset I")
off = [q.moved(w=-1.6) if q.key == "FB" else q for q in off]
dfn = base43(off, fix={"MIKE": dict(w=0.6), "SAM": dict(d=4.0, w=6.6)})
q1 = ring_by_body(Play(off, dfn, los=50, to_go=4))
fld = q1.draw(lateral=(-17.5, 17.5), window=(-9.0, 14.5), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(fld.ax)
plt.show()
```

**What formation and personnel is this? Run or pass? And which side is the fullback set up to lead
to?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**An offset I, offset weak (a "Weak I"), with 21 personnel.** Two backs (fullback and tailback) and one
tight end, so two receivers. The fullback is offset to the left, away from the tight end: that's
"weak."

**Run or pass:** lean run. Two backs stacked behind an under-center quarterback ran about three times in
four in neutral situations, and second-and-4 is a comfortable running down. If it's a pass, expect a
play fake.

**Which side:** the left. The offset fullback is already behind the left guard, in position to lead on a
weak-side run (an iso into the bubble over the Will, as in the iso diagram) or to pick up a blitzing
linebacker from that side on play-action. Whether *this* offense actually runs toward its offset is a
tendency, not a rule, and smart offenses break it on purpose. There's no league-wide number to look up:
the public charting data records how many backs there are, not which way the fullback is offset; that
takes tracking data ([Tracking Data and the Big Data
Bowl](../13-analytics-and-data/13-05-tracking-data-and-big-data-bowl.qmd) works with it). Log it for the team you're watching instead.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: second-and-goal at the 1"}
The offense has the ball on the defense's 1-yard line, second down. It sends in three tight ends, a
fullback and a tailback; the defense answers with its goal-line package.

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-gl
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: second-and-goal at the 1. The offense is in its goal-line formation; the tight end H is a wing behind and outside Y. The defense has five linemen, three linebackers and three defensive backs; its two safeties (SS, FS) are only about four yards deep."
q2 = ring_by_body(Play(players_of("Goal line"), gl_def, los=109, to_go=None))
fld = q2.draw(lateral=(-13.0, 13.0), window=(-9.0, 8.5), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(fld.ax)
plt.show()
```

**Count the blockers and the defenders in the box. Who wins the count, and so how does the offense
try to score? If it throws, who is the likeliest target?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The defense wins the count, eleven to nine,** and at the goal line it always will: nobody has to stay
deep. The offense's blockers are the five linemen, the three tight ends and the fullback; the
quarterback and the tailback don't block.

**So the offense doesn't try to block everyone.** It tries to win one gap. Expect a run aimed at a single
spot with extra bodies there (a double team and the fullback leading into the hole) or a quarterback
sneak behind the center. A tailback who needs one yard only has to fall forward.

**If it throws:** a play fake and a tight end, because eleven defenders committed to the run is exactly
what the fake exploits. The likeliest target is the wing (H) or the tight end on the side away from the
fake: he blocks for a count, as he would on a run, then slips into the end zone while the linebackers
and safeties step up. Watch the two safeties: if both crash at the snap, the tight end is alone.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: the I against eight in the box"}
First-and-10 at midfield, second quarter. The offense is in the I with 21 personnel. The defense, in
its base 4-3, has walked the strong safety down beside the linebackers, leaving one safety deep.

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-box
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: I-formation (21 personnel) against a base 4-3 with the strong safety (SS) walked down outside the Sam linebacker on the tight end's side, leaving one deep safety (FS) in the middle of the field. The cornerbacks (C) are about seven yards off the two receivers."
off = players_of("I-formation")
dfn = base43(off, shell="single_high", fix={"SS": dict(d=5.5, w=8.8), "SAM": dict(d=4.0, w=5.6),
                                            "MIKE": dict(w=0.6), "FS": dict(d=13.5)})
q3 = ring_by_body(Play(off, dfn, los=60, to_go=10))
q3.highlight("SS", "FS", color=style.DEFENSE)
fld = q3.draw(lateral=(-17.5, 17.5), window=(-9.0, 16.0), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(fld.ax)
plt.show()
```

**Do the count. Why did the defense bring the safety down, and what is the offense likely to try?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The count is eight against seven.** The offense has seven blockers (five linemen, the tight end and the
fullback). In the box the defense has four linemen, three linebackers and the strong safety: eight. The
I's whole advantage was a hat on a hat with a lead blocker; the safety takes that away by giving the
defense one more player than the offense can block. It came down because the formation says run.

**What the offense is likely to try:** the run is still the most common call. If it runs, it often runs
*away* from the extra man, to the left here: the safety walked down on the tight end's side, so a run
the other way makes him chase across the formation, and he arrives late. But this is also the picture
play-action was invented for. Single-high, with the safety in the middle, means each cornerback is alone
on his side, with no safety beside him. If the defense is playing man coverage behind the safety
([Cover 1](../06-pass-coverage/06-02-man-coverage.qmd)), that's a one-on-one outside; if it's zone with
the corners dropping deep ([Cover 3](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd)), the fake pulls the
linebackers up and opens the window behind them for a crossing route. Either way, the run fake is what
moves the eight defenders.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **The classic formations are defined by the backfield.** Read them back to front: quarterback under
  center or not, how many backs, and whether they're stacked (I), side by side (pro set), offset
  (offset I) or three wide (T, wishbone, Power I).
- **Each formation is an answer to a problem, and every answer has a price.** The I gives the tailback a
  lead blocker and a running start but is slow to the edge and obvious; the pro set is balanced and
  quick-hitting but has no deep tailback; the singleback and ace trade the fullback for a tight end or receiver; the wishbone and
  flexbone are built to read a defender instead of blocking him; the Wing-T lives on misdirection; the
  goal-line formation trades all its space for blockers.
- **They're one family.** The T's three backs were stacked (I), split (pro set), spread (flexbone),
  scattered for misdirection (Wing-T) or traded for receivers (singleback). Knowing the tree helps you
  name the shape.
- **Count, every time.** Blockers (everyone but the quarterback and the ball carrier) against defenders
  in the box. A hat on a hat favors the run; one extra defender is the defense's answer; at the goal
  line the defense always wins the count, so the offense picks one gap instead.
- **Formation follows personnel.** 21 usually means an I, offset I or pro set; 12 an ace; 11 a
  singleback or a shotgun look; three backs or three tight ends mean short yardage. Name the shape by
  where players stand, the personnel by who they are.
- **Two-back, under-center football faded because passing won, and it survives where running and
  faking matter most.** In 2025, under center meant run about 70% of the time, play-action on about
  four of five dropbacks, and it was the default on short yardage. The under-center share rose to about
  a third of plays as offenses got bigger against lighter defenses.
